+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 66.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur Neegan sat in the transfer vessel's passenger compartment, his boots pressed flat against a deck plate that hummed with residual reactor vibration. A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text. "Pressure nominal. Hull integrity nominal. Social tension," he muttered, "not nominal." The screen ticked along: coolant, shielding, grav compensation, radiation count. Outside, the transfer ship held course through the dark, its hull marked with no company logo, no colonial flag, only a faint serial number that looked more like a legal citation than an identification. The air smelled of recycled oxygen and polished metal, the particular scent of places where important decisions were made before anyone admitted they were being made quietly. Behind him, two men in charcoal jumpsuits stood with the patient posture of guards who had been told to look bored. Their cuffs bore the Antares diplomatic seal: a silver circle bisected by a blue band, with a stylized star at its center. Diplomatic, Arthur thought. At the far end of the compartment, a woman sat with her hands folded in her lap. "Mr. Neegan," she said. "Ms. Vail?" "You have the right not to answer questions. You do not have the right to remain on that plot indefinitely." Arthur looked at the ceiling. "I'm not a corporation. I'm an engineer. I found a vein under my house." "Then you are in possession of an unregistered strategic deposit." "Under the Colonial Charter, surface discoveries belong to the settler for a period of—" "Which charter, Mr. Neegan?" He stopped. She smiled without warmth. "There are three. The old Terran Mining Statutes, the Martian Compact, and the Antares Interstellar Accord. Which one do you intend to cite?" Arthur had the unpleasant sensation of a trap closing around his feet. "The one that says I can keep my home." "That one has not been ratified by the Interstellar Council." "Then why am I being asked to leave my home?" "Because you are being asked to make a decision." "Who are you working for?" he asked. "Antares Diplomatic Corps." "Right." "Antares is a neutral station, Mr. Neegan. We manage negotiations between the mining syndicates, the Terran fleets, and the colonial governments. We do not take sides." "Then why are there armed men in my house?" "They are here for your protection." "From whom?" "From those who believe that Azra should not be divided." Arthur looked at her. "Azra is a metal." "An unstable one." "It accelerates decay. That's what the mining pamphlets say." "That is what the public version says." She leaned forward slightly. "Azra does not merely accelerate decay. It alters the probability field of radioactive transitions. In small quantities, it makes drives efficient. In large quantities, it makes weapons unpredictable. In the wrong quantities, it can make a starship's reactor fail in a matter of seconds." Arthur felt the cold of the compartment settle into his shoulders. "You're saying it's dangerous." "I'm saying it is valuable enough to start wars." Arthur said, "There are people on Mars who depend on those drives. Colonies, hospitals, freighters. If Azra can make travel safer—" "Then it must be controlled." "By whom?" "By those willing to bear the responsibility." Arthur laughed once, sharply. "That's what every corporation says before they sign a lease." "Corporations bear the cost. Governments bear the blame. Engineers bear the consequences." She said it flatly, without accusation. "Your plot sits on a vein that extends for several kilometers. The core samples you took were taken without authorization. The readings you transmitted were intercepted. Three mining companies have filed claims. Two military attachés have requested your detention. One senator has asked for your plot to be declared a protected cultural site." "Cultural site?" "A convenient fiction. It would freeze the land while the legal questions are settled." Arthur thought of his mother's garden, the thin red soil, the first house he had ever owned. "They can't just take it." "They can. But they will not, if you agree to a meeting." The question came out before he could stop it. "Who?" The woman reached into a side pouch and placed a small card on the table. It was plain, without a name, but embossed with the same silver circle and blue band. "The meeting is off-world. A private station. You will be escorted by the Antares Diplomatic Corps. You will be offered a choice." "What choice?" "Whether to become a symbol, a witness, or a partner." Arthur stared at the card. "A partner in what?" "In understanding what Azra is." The vessel's lights dimmed for a second, then returned. The screen changed again: destination trajectory confirmed. Arthur looked at the guards, at the woman, at the card. He thought of the drilling rigs outside his window, the corporate surveyors with their polite smiles, the indentured laborers waiting at the gates for leases that would bind their children to the dust. He thought of the way the ore had glowed faintly when he first broke through the cap rock, as if the metal remembered some older fire. "If I refuse?" he asked. "Then you remain on Mars. And Mars remains what it is." "A mine?" "A prize." Arthur picked up the card. "Where is this station?" "Beyond the asteroid belt. Neutral ground." "Neutral," he said, "is a word people use when they have already chosen." The woman stood. "The meeting will begin in six hours. You will be given a suit, a credential, and a list of questions you are not to ask. You will also be given a small device. If you press it, a signal will be sent to the station. They will know you have arrived. They will also know you are afraid." Arthur looked at the screen. The green text continued its endless cycle. "Is that a threat?" "It is a courtesy." "Then I suppose I'd better not be afraid." The woman smiled, and for the first time it looked almost human. "No, Mr. Neegan. I suppose you would not."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a solid grasp of Asimovian science fiction conventions while delivering the requested scenario effectively. The author successfully captures the classic sci-fi atmosphere through technical details, political intrigue, and the characteristic blend of personal stakes with galactic implications that defines Asimov's work. The dialogue carries the narrative well, with Ms. Vail serving as an effective exposition vehicle while maintaining an appropriately mysterious and bureaucratic tone. Her responses feel authentically diplomatic - revealing information while obscuring true motives. Arthur's reactions are believable for an ordinary person thrust into extraordinary circumstances, though his characterization remains somewhat surface-level. The world-building effectively establishes the complex political landscape through details like competing charters, multiple claiming parties, and the neutral Antares station. The revelation about Azra's true properties beyond simple decay acceleration adds appropriate scientific intrigue. The technical descriptions of the ship and its systems provide authentic sci-fi atmosphere without becoming overly dense. However, the piece suffers from some structural issues. The pacing feels uneven, with important revelations delivered in rapid succession during dialogue exchanges. Some exposition feels forced, particularly when Ms. Vail explains the various legal frameworks and Azra's properties. The ending, while attempting to show Arthur's resolve, feels somewhat abrupt and doesn't fully capitalize on the tension built throughout the scene. The prose is generally competent but lacks distinctive flair. Descriptions are functional rather than evocative, and while the dialogue serves its purpose, it occasionally veers toward the mechanical. The piece successfully avoids purple prose but at the cost of some emotional resonance. Arthur's internal conflict about losing his home and the broader implications could have been explored more deeply. The political intrigue is well-established, with hints of larger forces at play, though the stakes could feel more immediate and personal. The piece succeeds in creating questions about Arthur's future choices while maintaining the requested retrofuturistic atmosphere. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The red darkroom lamp turned everything the color of wine, and I stood at the enlarger trying to remember how to be in control. I, Dani, am twenty-five, an art student who has built a bold style and a take-charge attitude in relationships, the kind of person who names desire before it can hide. For the past semester, I had been quietly fascinated by Elliot, a nineteen-year-old boy in my experimental photography class. He wore killer thrift-shop-nu-goth: velvet, lace, boots too large, a soft demeanour, and a quiet intellect that made the room lean closer without noise in the dark. Our final project required a series of portraits, and the professor paired us with a casualness that felt like fate. Late nights followed. The darkroom became a confessional: red light, trays, the smell of chemicals, and the slow reveal of images in the bath. Elliot stood beside me, careful and warm, while I fixed the paper, set the timer, and tried to keep my voice steady. There was a tender awkwardness between us, the kind that happens when two people are learning how to share a small space without stepping on each other's shadows while the small fan ticked low. Elliot hummed a soft tune while waiting for the images to reveal in the chemical bath. It was not a song with words, only a low line that moved under the silence. I watched his mouth, then his hands, then the paper lifting from the solution. The tune made my pulse do something stupid. I am used to taking charge, to steering conversations and bodies toward clarity, but this quiet melody pulled me into a different rhythm. For the first time, I wanted to be led, even if only for the length of one developing print in the red dark. I had always been drawn to more defined gender presentations: broad shoulders, hard jawlines, the confident architecture of a man who knew exactly what he was. Elliot unsettled me because he did not announce himself. His masculinity was unconventional, gentle, and thoughtful, a puzzle I wanted to solve without solving. I felt excited, almost giddy, at the thought that I was witnessing his self-discovery. At the same time, I felt confused. If my attraction relied on certainty, what did I do with a person who was becoming? I did not want to flatten him into something I already knew well. One night, after the third print had dried, Elliot set down the tongs and looked at the tray as if it might answer for him. 'I need to tell you something,' he said. His voice was small, but not weak. 'I have been questioning my gender identity and expression. The way I dress, the way I move, the parts of being a boy that feel inherited instead of chosen.' He paused, watching me. I wanted to take charge, to reassure him, to make the moment safe. Instead, I held still and let his words land where they needed to, now. My usual assertiveness felt dangerous. I wanted to protect Elliot's vulnerability, to wrap it in promises and control, but I also knew that protection could become possession. He was not a project to fix, even though our final assignment demanded images. I had to give him agency, even when my hands ached to steer. The red light made my face look less certain than I felt. I am someone who takes charge, but I was learning that taking charge sometimes means asking what the other person needs, and then trusting the answer without making it about me, all at once. Chemistry arrived without warning, in the space between our hands over the print. He would ask about exposure, and I would answer, but the questions were no longer only about light. 'Do you feel safe here?' he asked once, and the question hung in the red air. I laughed, then stopped, because laughter felt too bright. 'I do,' I said, 'but I am not sure I have done it before.' He nodded, as if that were enough, and the tenderness of the moment made my chest ache. We were both in uncharted territory, and it did not frighten us yet. I was not used to being unmoored. My identity had always been built on boldness: I knew what I wanted, I pursued it, and I made room for it. Elliot made me question whether that certainty was strength or armor. I was attracted to him, but not in the simple way I expected. I was attracted to his softness, his intelligence, his willingness to be uncertain. I was excited to witness his self-discovery, and I was terrified that my excitement might make me careless with him. I did not want to rush him or make him small in the dark. 'What do you want me to do?' I asked, because I could not stand the not-knowing. Elliot looked at the bath, where a new image was slowly appearing. 'Tell me what you want,' he said. 'But do not decide for me.' I swallowed. 'I want to be here. I want to be careful. I want to know if you are interested, and I want you to have the space to say yes, no, or maybe.' The words were not a command. They were an offering, and that frightened me more than silence. It felt true and new to me now. Elliot hummed the soft tune again as the image finished revealing, the shadows deepening into a face I almost recognized. He held the print under the water, then lifted it, and for a moment we both stopped breathing. 'Stay?' he asked. I wanted to answer with the old boldness, the take-charge certainty I had built my life around. Instead, I let my hand rest near his, not touching, but close enough to feel the heat. 'Stay,' I said. In the red dark, we were both becoming. The red light held us like a secret neither of us had named yet.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, capturing Dani's perspective as she navigates her attraction to Elliot during their darkroom sessions. The author successfully establishes the confessional atmosphere of the red-lit darkroom and explores the complex dynamics between the characters. The characterization is nuanced and believable. Dani's internal struggle between her natural assertiveness and her desire to give Elliot agency feels authentic and well-developed. Her confusion about her own identity when faced with Elliot's gender questioning is psychologically realistic. Elliot emerges as a fully realized character despite limited dialogue, with his vulnerability and thoughtfulness clearly conveyed. The prose demonstrates considerable elegance, with evocative imagery like "The red darkroom lamp turned everything the color of wine" and "his masculinity was unconventional, gentle, and thoughtful, a puzzle I wanted to solve without solving." The darkroom setting is used effectively as both literal space and metaphor for the characters' emotional territory. However, the piece suffers from some stylistic issues. Certain phrases feel overwrought, such as "made my pulse do something stupid" and the repeated use of "in the dark" as a rhythmic ending. Some sentences become convoluted in their attempt at poetic language, occasionally sacrificing clarity for style. The dialogue, while limited, feels natural and serves the story well. Elliot's confession about questioning his gender identity is handled with appropriate sensitivity, and the conversation flows believably between the characters. The emotional complexity is well-executed, particularly Dani's realization that "taking charge sometimes means asking what the other person needs." The piece avoids easy resolutions while still providing a satisfying sense of connection between the characters. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - hopeful but uncertain, reflecting the characters' emotional states without forcing premature resolution. The transformation in Dani's understanding feels earned through the careful buildup of her internal conflict. Some minor weaknesses include occasional redundancy in phrasing and moments where the prose becomes slightly precious, but these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Stolen Moments in Roma The Trevi Fountain was a riot of elbows, cameras, and bad advice. Ben held his guidebook open like a shield, reciting the dimensions of the sea horse, when a matte-black motorcycle hissed around the corner like a black cat with a grudge. Alessandra did not brake. She swerved, one boot scraping stone, and stopped three inches from his knee. “Scusa,” she said, in English with a knife in it. “You are standing in the path of a woman with a deadline.” “I’m so sorry,” Ben said. “I was only—” “Only what? Reading? Here? Among the pigeons?” She gestured at the crowd. “You look like a lost comma.” He blinked. “I beg your pardon?” “I said you look like a lost comma. Small, polite, and completely in the wrong sentence.” She looked down at her phone. “Damn it. If I miss this delivery, my cousin will call me again. You have a car?” “I don’t drive in Rome.” “Good. Then you’re useless but available.” She kicked the stand down. “Get on.” “I—what?” “Back. Now. Before I change my mind.” He should have said no. He was on sabbatical, in Rome for a week, with a notebook full of footnotes and a heart that had been orderly for years. Instead, he climbed onto the back of the motorcycle, arms uncertain, and felt the city lurch under them. “Where are we going?” he shouted over the engine. “Wherever the day decides.” She took him first to the Spanish Steps, not to sit, but to race a scooter up the staircase. Ben clutched her waist as they climbed, then descended, then stopped at a café where Alessandra ordered two espresso without asking. “You drink?” she asked. “I didn’t know if I could.” “Life is a thing you drink before you know if you can.” She sipped hers in one go, then palmed a marble from a child’s game near the table. Ben saw. He did not say anything. At Campo de’ Fiori, she made him taste a fried artichoke from a cone. He burned his tongue. She laughed, not cruelly, but with the bright surprise of a bird escaping a cage. “You have a very serious face for a man with pepper in his mouth,” she said. “I’m a historian.” “Of what?” “Of nothing important, apparently.” She winked. They moved through the city like a rumor. She stopped at a bookshop and lifted a pen from a display, rolling it between her fingers. At a flower stall, she took a red carnation from a bucket and tucked it behind Ben’s ear. “You look like a tourist now,” she said. “I feel like a criminal.” “Better.” They ran into Marco near the Tiber, an old acquaintance with a tattooed forearm and a scooter leaning against the wall. He saw Ben first, then Alessandra, and his expression became a warning. “Ben,” Marco said, in careful English. “You are with Alessandra?” “I am.” Marco looked at her. “Alessandra, you are doing the thing.” “What thing?” she asked. “The thing where you find a person who is too polite to run and you make him feel alive.” Ben turned to her. “Is that true?” Alessandra shrugged. “I make people feel Rome. It is not my fault Rome is dangerous.” Marco leaned closer to Ben. “She is brilliant. She is also a fire you do not hold. She will take your wallet, your heart, maybe your left shoe. Leave before sunset.” Alessandra smiled, all teeth. “Marco, you are jealous. You have not stolen anything interesting in years.” Marco laughed. “I stole a whole pizza once.” “That was embarrassing.” Ben, still holding the espresso cup, felt something shift under his ribs. He had come to Rome to study the city from a distance, through dates and citations. Alessandra had handed him a pen, a flower, a stolen marble, and an engine. “Where next?” he asked. She looked at him for a long moment. Her eyes were dark, quick, amused. “Somewhere you will not like.” “I like not liking.” She grinned. “Then climb on.” They went to Trastevere after dark. She parked near a courtyard where a band played accordion and a woman was selling lemon cakes. Alessandra led Ben inside, past tables of laughing strangers, to a stone bench under a pergola. The air smelled of basil, warm stone, and river water. “You are quiet,” she said. “I am trying to decide if I am in a dream.” “Good. Dreams are easier to leave.” “You are leaving.” She did not answer. She set the red carnation on the bench between them, then the marble, then the pen. Three small objects, arranged like a secret. Ben stared at them. “What are those for?” “For you. In case you forget.” “Forget what?” “That for one day, you were not a comma.” He wanted to say something clever, something scholarly, something safe. Instead he said, “I think I remember.” She touched his wrist, briefly, as if testing whether he was real. “You are very strange, Ben.” “So I am told.” “By Marco?” “By everyone.” She laughed, low and warm. “Good. I hate normal.” A busker began to play something old and sweet. The courtyard filled with light. Alessandra leaned closer, and for a moment the city outside ceased to exist; there was only her breath, the heat of her skin, the faint scent of motor oil and citrus. “Will you come back?” she asked. “Tomorrow?” “When.” He looked at the objects on the bench, then at her. “If you promise to steal something.” “I promise nothing.” “Then I will have to steal you first.” She stared at him, then smiled, slow and dangerous. “You are learning.” They did not kiss. Not yet. But as she stood and brushed the carnation from the bench, she took his hand and led him out into the Roman night, streetlamps turning the cobblestones into gold. Behind them, the marble, the pen, and the flower remained on the stone bench, waiting like small promises.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniac tendencies are woven subtly throughout the narrative through specific actions (taking the marble, pen, carnation) rather than being explicitly stated, showing sophisticated restraint. The dialogue crackles with personality - Alessandra's sharp wit ("You look like a lost comma") and Ben's evolving confidence create authentic chemistry. The cultural clash is well-rendered without resorting to stereotypes, and both characters feel genuinely three-dimensional. Ben's transformation from timid academic to someone willing to engage with danger feels earned through the progression of scenes. The prose style is confident and evocative, with particularly strong imagery ("motorcycle hissed around the corner like a black cat with a grudge," "streetlamps turning the cobblestones into gold"). The writing maintains consistent voice throughout while allowing each character's distinct speech patterns to emerge naturally. The structure effectively uses interconnected vignettes to build tension and chemistry. The pacing moves briskly without feeling rushed, and each scene serves both plot advancement and character development. The introduction of Marco provides external perspective that enriches our understanding of Alessandra without feeling forced. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - romantic tension without premature resolution, leaving the reader wanting more while providing satisfying closure to this particular day. The symbolic objects left on the bench create a poetic resonance that feels earned rather than overwrought. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the dialogue becomes slightly too polished for natural speech, and some metaphors that border on precious. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Last Outpost hums at a lazy 54 hertz. I keep the bar polished, the lights low, and the complaints filed where they belong. Tonight it smells of cinnamon coolant, stale coffee, and recycled air. I'm wiping the same spot when the stranger plops down. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Her tentacles are frayed dreads, askew, her skin blue-gray. She looks like she's been through a hull breach and a laundry cycle. "First or second double?" I ask. "First. The second one's for when I'm dead." I pour. Vega whisky burns like an engine start. I slide the glass across. "Name?" "Kestrel. Or don't ask." "I ask. It's bar policy." "Then you can write it down and use it to file your complaints." I don't write it down. I keep wiping the same spot, a small dark circle near the edge. "You look like you've got a problem," I say. "Problem's got a ship, a warrant, and a very bad temper. She's called Vex." "Vex is a name, not a diagnosis." "She's a collector. I borrowed something from her." "Then pay her back." "I can't. It's not money." "What is it?" "A data seed. Small, warm, and currently singing in my jacket like a trapped bird." I stop wiping. The rag stays flat under my hand. "Where?" "Here." She taps her chest. "If they scan me, they'll hear it." A miner clears his throat. "Nets, you got a problem?" "Quiet, Orin. Private conversation." "Everything here is private until it isn't." "Then make it private." Orin shrugs, but his eyes stay on Kestrel's twitching tentacles. Kestrel leans in. "I need a place to hide." "Not here." "Your back room. The one with the old med bay." "That's not a hiding place. It's a storage closet with a broken bed." "It's behind a wall that doesn't show on my scanners." "Because I keep the scanners broken." "See? You're already helping." "I'm keeping the peace. There's a difference." The comm chimes. I don't answer. It chimes again, polite. "Who is that?" Kestrel asks. "Nobody." "It says 'Last Outpost, this is Vex. You have a guest. Return her, or we'll start asking your patrons very personal questions.'" I look at the comm, at Kestrel, at the same spot, polished like a little moon. "You didn't hear that," I say. "I heard it loud enough." "Good. Then you know the rules." "The rules are: no fights, no weapons, no talking about the past." "And no bringing trouble to the door." "I brought trouble to the door. I'm sorry. I didn't know the door was this quiet." "It's quiet because I keep it that way." "Then keep it that way." "I can't keep a ship out of the sky." "No. But you can keep me out of sight." The room leans in. Mirel, merchant in gold thread, watches from the end of the bar. Her fingers tap an expensive rhythm. "Mirel," I say, "you're buying a round if this gets ugly." "I'm buying a round if you let me buy a round." "Deal." Mirel smiles. "I like you, Nets. You're always so certain you're not involved." "I am not involved." "Yet." Kestrel's glass is empty. I pour another without being asked. "Tell me what you stole," I say. "A manifest. A list of ships that were paid to disappear. Vex's people think it's in a vault. It's not. It's in me." "Why?" "Because someone has to carry it, and I'm the only one who can hide it where they can't scan it." "Where's that?" "Inside the seed. It's not just data. It's a living archive. It feeds on heat. If I get scared, it sings louder." Her tentacles tremble. The whisky shivers. "Is it singing now?" "Yes." "Can you stop it?" "No. Can you?" "What happens if it sings too loud?" "It becomes a beacon. Vex will find me by the sound." "Then we need to make it stop." "I can't make it stop. I can only make it quieter." "Whisky?" "Help." "Whisky first." "You're the barkeeper." "I'm the only barkeeper." "That's what I thought." I wipe the same spot. Circle, circle, circle. "No," I say. Outside, the belt turns in slow, cold rings. Somewhere beyond the dust, a ship is holding position, patient as a debt. The bar's old heater coughs, and the ceiling lights flicker in a pattern I recognize all too well. The door opens. Cold air smells of dust and ozone. A man steps in, face too many angles, black coat hem steaming. "Last Outpost," he says. His voice is flat, but his eyes are not. "We're looking for a woman with tentacles and a bad habit of stealing." Kestrel goes very still. I keep wiping. "Sit down," I say to him. "Buy a drink. Then ask your questions." "I'm not here to drink." "Everyone's here to drink. That's the only law." He looks at Kestrel. The seed in her jacket hums, a thin wire about to snap. "Last chance," the man says. "Hand her over, and this place stays exactly as it is." I set the rag down, pick it up, wipe the same spot. "Ask me a question," I say. "If I like the answer, I'll tell you something." The man blinks. "What kind of question?" "Any question." "Where is she?" I smile, the smile I use when gravity plates act up. "I don't know who you're talking about." His eyes move to Kestrel. Her tentacles curl inward, a flower closing. "That," I say, "was the answer." The comm chimes again. Not Vex. The station's warning tone: outer doors sealing. Mirel stands. "Nets, you started this." "No," I say. "I'm just finishing the round." The door is closed, the light red, and the man reaches under his coat. I keep wiping the same spot on the bar counter. "Kestrel," I say, "if you have a plan, now's the time." "I have a seed, a whisky, and a very bad idea." "Good enough." The man's hand moves. I don't stop wiping.

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. Every time I tug it back, I feel like I'm pulling myself together. New Orleans hits different: river water, old paper, something sweet burning. The sun is too friendly. I have been here since last night, but my brain is still in the parking lot where the van driver tossed my duffel like I was garbage. "You're not going anywhere, kid." I am going somewhere. I'm here. My name is Taylor, but I haven't said it out loud in two days. In Tennessee, Taylor was a problem. In New Orleans, maybe it's just a name. I walk. My pockets are light. I have fourteen dollars, a dead phone, a wrong map, and a backpack that keeps trying to leave me. The strap slips. I tug it. My neck aches from holding my head up like I belong. I need water. I need a bathroom. I need to know if people are kind or dangerous. New Orleans makes you feel seen and sold. My mom said, "We don't have room for that in this family." Not "I'm scared." Not "I love you." Room. As if I were furniture. The backpack strap slips again. I catch it with both hands and stand there, looking ridiculous. "You're doing it wrong," someone says. I turn. A girl, maybe my age, sits on the curb. Dark hair, jagged. Yellow tank top, hole in the shoulder. Sneakers that look like they've crossed state lines. Her eyes are sharp. Maybe mean. Hard to tell. "Doing what wrong?" I ask. "Standing there like you're waiting for permission." She points at my backpack. "That thing's stealing your posture." I look down. The strap is hanging off one shoulder. "Thanks. I was just—" "Trying not to cry?" My throat closes. "No." "Okay. I'm Marisol." She says it like a door opening. I don't say my name. That feels important. "Taylor," I finally say. She nods. "Taylor. That's a good name for someone who's about to do something stupid." I almost laugh. "That's the first nice thing anyone's said to me in two days." Marisol's face changes, just a little. "Yeah? What did they say?" I tell her about the van driver. I don't tell her about my mom. Not yet. Marisol listens with her chin in her hands, and when I finish, she says, "You came to New Orleans with no plan." "It was a plan," I say. "It was a panic." "It was a plan made by panic." She grins. "I like that. I like panic." We walk together. She knows the city like a secret code. She tells me which corners to avoid, which people to pretend not to see, which places will let you drink fountain water. "The fountain near the old church," she says. "Nobody cares. The woman with the blue scarf? She'll give you a pretzel if you smile." "Why are you telling me this?" I ask. Marisol shrugs. "Because you're new and you look like you're about to make a mistake." "What mistake?" "Trusting the wrong person." I stop walking. "You're the wrong person?" Her grin fades. "Maybe. Maybe not. That's the fun part." I hate that I want to believe her. I hate that I'm so tired of being careful that I'd rather be scared and alive. My backpack strap slips. I tug it. Marisol notices. "You need a break," she says. We sit on a bench under a tree. Marisol pulls a granola bar out of her bag. It's bent. She offers me half. I take it. It tastes like cardboard and sugar, and I'm grateful. "Where are you from?" she asks. "Tennessee." "Backwater?" "Very." "Family problem?" I chew slowly. "Identity problem." She nods. "Oh. That's a family problem." I look at her. "You say that like you know." Marisol's eyes go away for a second. "I know a lot of things. I just don't get to use them." "Like what?" "Like how to disappear." My stomach drops. "You're a runaway?" She laughs, but it's thin. "Runaway, homeless, lost, escaped, temporarily misplaced. People use a lot of words for the same thing." "How long?" "Long enough to be good at it." I want to ask if she's safe. I want to ask if she has a place to sleep. I want to ask if she's ever been hurt. Instead I say, "Do you have money?" She looks at me. "No." "Me neither." We sit in the quiet. A dog barks. A bus hisses. Marisol picks at the granola bar wrapper. "I sleep in a church basement sometimes," she says. "Not all the time. Not all the churches. There's a woman there who asks questions, but she asks them like she wants to help, not like she wants to catch you." "Is that safe?" "Safe is a lie we tell ourselves so we can keep walking." I hate how true that sounds. My phone buzzes. I almost panic. It's a text from my mom: WHERE ARE YOU. I stare at the letters. My hands shake. I turn it off. Marisol sees. "You don't have to answer." "I don't know who to trust." She points at me. "Start with the person who gives you half a granola bar." "That's not a lot of trust." "It's a start." The sun starts to go down. New Orleans turns gold and purple. The air gets heavy. I feel the city pressing against me, all its music and heat and danger. I need a place to sleep. I need a shower. I need someone to tell me my name is okay. I need to be brave, but bravery feels like a coat that doesn't fit. Marisol stands. "Come on. I know a spot." "Where?" "You don't need to know yet." My backpack strap slips off my shoulder. I let it hang there for a second. Then I pick it up, tuck it under my arm, and follow her. I don't know if I'm making a mistake. I don't know if Marisol is kind or dangerous. I don't know if New Orleans will save me or swallow me. But for the first time in two days, I'm not walking alone, and that feels like a door cracking open. The street lights come on. Marisol's shadow stretches long in front of me. I step into it, and for now, that is enough. I am not alone tonight.

+ Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world had not arrived with thunder. It had arrived with administrative disappointment, as if the sky had filed a complaint and gone home. This was useful, Midas thought, because it meant there was no one to blame except everyone. He sat on a crate labelled FRAGILE in a language no one still spoke, staring at the valley below. The sun was doing its best, which meant shining through ash, old smoke, and the general suspicion that it had been replaced by a slightly less competent model. Chewy sat beside him. Chewy was a stuffed koala of animo-tronic construction, from the Before Time, when machines spoke while appearing to be made of felt, buttons, and optimistic fluff. His left ear was bent at an angle that suggested he had once witnessed a miracle and was still deciding whether to believe in it. “We need water,” Midas said. Chewy blinked his button eyes. “We need water,” Midas repeated, “because if we don’t find water, the goats will look at us with hope that usually precedes litigation.” Chewy’s panel glowed a cheerful blue. Then, in a voice like a radio station trapped in a friendly throat, he said, “Hydrate your dreams! Now with thirty percent more feeling!” “Quality assurance is a lifestyle,” Chewy added. Chewy had been found in a ruined shopping arcade, half-buried in shoes that once promised to walk you into tomorrow. He had been dead, or convincingly unconscious, until Midas kicked him while looking for fungus. Chewy had opened one eye and said, “Warranty void if seal is broken,” which had started a friendship neither fully understood. Home Base, a stone wall, a leaky roof, a goat, and the shared belief that the outside was worse, had been low on water for two days. The cistern leak appeared to be caused less by engineering failure and more by the universe making a point. The point was that he was bad at planning. “The spring is over the ridge,” Midas said. “We leave before the sun gets mean, fill the barrels, and are back before the goats unionize.” Chewy’s ears twitched. “Do not let your day be merely adequate.” “Thank you,” Midas said. “I’ll try to let it be adequately disastrous.” They set out with two barrels, a rope, a knife, a banner for Brainy Munchies, and confidence that was mostly decorative. The road had been swallowed by weeds and old vehicle bones. Midas had a knack for trouble, and the world arranged its hazards accordingly. The first problem was a ravine. It had not been there the previous week. Now it yawned across the path with the casual confidence of a chasm waiting for someone stupid to pass by. “Bridge,” Midas said. There was no bridge. There was, however, a tree, a rope, and a branch that looked as if it had been holding on out of spite. Chewy examined the branch. “This product has been tested by people who were not entirely awake.” Midas tied the rope to the branch, tested it, and tested it again, because testing was the only thing standing between him and the ground. He swung. For one brief, glorious moment, he was airborne. Then the branch made a sound like a disappointed accordion and let go. Midas landed in brambles that had clearly been waiting for him personally. He emerged, bleeding slightly, with a leaf in his hair and a new appreciation for other people’s decisions. Chewy, who had not swung, stood at the edge of the ravine, looking at him with the patience of a customer service representative. They found the spring, smaller, muddier, and more guarded than expected. A badger had established a presence there with the authority of a landlord who had never intended to leave. Midas attempted to negotiate. The badger attempted to bite his hand. The negotiation ended quickly. Chewy, seeing an opportunity to be useful, said, “Premium hydration for premium customers only.” Midas, not missing the chance, said, “What’s your name?” The badger did not answer. It looked at him with the irritation of a creature interrupted during a very important bite. In the end, they filled the barrels by taking turns: Midas held the badger at bay with a stick, and Chewy recited slogans until the badger, baffled, moved to a more promising patch of dirt. It was not a victory, exactly. It was the sort of thing that happened when two parties agreed to stop pretending. On the way home, the barrels became a problem. The first barrel broke on a rock. The second, which had been leaking from the beginning, developed a strategic reduction in capacity. The water sloshed out in a manner that suggested it had opinions. Chewy said, “Every drop counts.” They continued with the second barrel, now half-full, and a growing sense that the world was editing itself, removing inconvenient things until only the essentials remained. The essentials were Midas, Chewy, a goat that had followed them home, and a badger that had followed them out of curiosity. They reached Home Base in multiple ways, which was a phrase Midas used when he wanted to avoid explaining exactly how. First, he walked. Then he crawled. Then he rolled, because the goat had decided the barrel was a toy and the barrel had decided to be a wheel. Chewy, being animo-tronic, simply kept pace while emitting a soft, steady glow. Petra, the settlement’s only other resident, looked at them from the doorway. She kept the goats and the grudges. “You’re late.” “We had a ravine.” “And a badger.” “And a branch.” Chewy added, “Your day could be better.” Petra took the barrel, inspected it, and said, “Half the water, and a goat that thinks it owns us.” Midas looked at the goat. The goat chewed with the slow satisfaction of a creature that had been right all along. “I feel worse for wear,” Midas said. Chewy’s panel dimmed to amber. “You’re worth a warranty.” It was, he decided, the closest comfort left behind.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical observations, and ability to find profound meaning in mundane post-apocalyptic survival. The author successfully creates a world where the apocalypse arrived "with administrative disappointment," immediately establishing the Pratchettesque tone of bureaucratic absurdity applied to cosmic events. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a believably hapless protagonist whose self-awareness about his predicament adds depth without becoming overly introspective. Chewy, the animatronic koala spouting corporate slogans, serves as both comic relief and a poignant reminder of the lost consumer culture. The dialogue between them feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and providing humor. The story structure adheres well to the prompt's requirements, beginning with deliberation, following the mission as it goes sideways, and returning the characters home "worse for wear." The mission's failures feel organic rather than forced - the missing bridge, the territorial badger, the leaking barrels all contribute to a cascade of minor disasters that feel authentically Pratchettesque. The prose demonstrates considerable skill in balancing humor with genuine pathos. Lines like "The sun was doing its best, which meant shining through ash, old smoke, and the general suspicion that it had been replaced by a slightly less competent model" showcase the author's ability to create vivid imagery while maintaining the wry tone throughout. However, the piece occasionally relies too heavily on quirky descriptions at the expense of deeper emotional resonance. While the humor is consistent, some moments could benefit from allowing more genuine vulnerability to surface. The ending, while appropriately understated, feels somewhat rushed and could have used more development to fully earn its quiet poignancy. The world-building is economical but effective, creating a sense of a lived-in post-apocalyptic environment without over-explaining. The introduction of Petra and the settlement dynamics adds believable context without overwhelming the central narrative. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of Cwm Bookshop clanged just as the rain found the window. Rhys Vale came in sideways, hood up, sunglasses on, looking less like a man seeking shelter than a fugitive from a bad dream. Behind him, the street was already swelling with camera flashes. Elin was shelving poetry when she looked up. “We’re not a café,” she said. “And we don’t serve celebrity.” “I’m not asking for a flat white,” he said, voice too smooth for the narrow shop. “Just thirty seconds. Maybe a minute if you’re feeling merciful.” “I’ll pay for the minute.” “Deal.” “Thirty seconds is a lot of money in a place this size.” “I’ll buy the shop. I’ll buy the poetry, the postcards, the little ceramic dragon by the till.” Elin glanced at the dragon. “He’s not for sale.” “Of course he isn’t. He has taste.” “He has a chipped horn. That’s not taste, that’s history.” Rhys lowered the sunglasses just enough for her to see his eyes. “I like chipped things,” he said. “They’ve been somewhere.” “Everything in this shop has been somewhere. That’s rather the point.” From outside, a shutter clicked. Then another. “Can you dim the lights?” “Please.” “We can’t keep the lights down. We’re a bookshop.” “I know what you are. I can see the shelves.” He turned back to her. “You’re the owner?” “I’m the owner, the stockist, the cleaner, and the person who will politely ask you to leave if you block the doorway.” “It does look like a film still.” “That’s because you’re blocking the display of Welsh nature writing.” “Nature writing. My favourite.” “Don’t say that. You’re going to say you love it because it sounds calm and green and nothing like your life.” He smiled, but it didn’t land. “You’re perceptive.” “Mostly.” “I’m a bookseller. We read people for a living. Most of them need a novel before they need a drink.” A flash went off outside. Rhys’s jaw tightened. “Right. So. If I don’t leave, what do I do?” Elin looked at him, then at the window, then at the narrow gap behind the poetry shelves. “You can hide in the back. There’s a stockroom. It smells of damp cardboard and regret, but the paparazzi won’t go in there.” “Regret? You keep regret in stock too?” “It’s seasonal.” He followed her, brushing his shoulder against a shelf of travel guides. “Quietly.” She led him through a gap in the books and into a low room where boxes were stacked to the ceiling. A model railway ran along the top of a workbench, curving around a miniature slate quarry and a tiny chapel with a white door. Rhys stopped. For once, the charm went out of his voice. “Is that a gauge one?” Elin looked at him. “You know gauge one?” “I know it’s not gauge zero. I can tell by the ballast.” She stared. “Ballast?” “Little stones. You fake it with grit, but proper ballast is sorted by size and colour.” He was already crouching by the bench, careful, as if the whole world had narrowed to the track. “That quarry is good. Did you do the weathering yourself?” “Mostly.” “Mostly? That’s a bit like saying the sea is mostly wet.” Elin felt something warm and inconvenient move behind her ribs. She crossed her arms. “I painted the chapel at two in the morning after a delivery van broke down. So don’t make it sound like art.” “It sounds like art.” “It sounds like a woman losing an argument with a ladder.” He looked up, and his smile was smaller now. “Do you do a lot of things at two in the morning?” “Enough to know how they taste.” Outside, the rain drummed on the skylight. In the shop front, a camera flash strobed again, but the sound was muffled, distant. Rhys ran a finger along the edge of the track without touching the train. “I built one once. Terrible. I was on location in Cornwall, bored, and I thought, what’s the worst thing a famous man can do in a quiet village?” “Buy a model railway and make a mess of it.” “And?” “I made a mess of it.” “Naturally.” “Of course you did.” “Then I fixed it. Badly. But I fixed it.” He looked at her. “Do you fix things badly?” “Only when I’m being modest.” “Ah. There it is.” “Don’t ‘there it is’ me.” He grinned, but it was a real grin, the kind that made his face look younger and less like a cover. “You like the trains.” “I like making small things that don’t need me to perform for them.” The words came out sharper than she intended. Rhys didn’t flinch. “That’s a very honest thing to say in a room full of books.” “Too true.” “Books don’t ask you to be charming.” “No, but they do ask you to be still.” She looked at the miniature chapel again. The white door was no bigger than her thumbnail. “Stillness is overrated.” “Is it? Or do you just pretend it is because you’re afraid of what you might hear if you stopped moving?” The silence between them changed. Elin felt it land in her chest before she could argue with it. “You read too much,” she said. “I read what I need to.” “And what do you need?” He was quiet for a moment. “To be liked. It’s embarrassing, isn’t it? For someone who looks like this.” He gestured vaguely at his own face. “Everyone thinks I’m full of myself. And I am, a little. But mostly I’m just hungry for the next yes.” “The next smile that isn’t for the cameras. The next person who’ll look at me and not see the name first.” Elin studied him. The famous face was there, yes, but so was the man crouched by the model railway, careful with his hands. “You’re not very good at this,” she said. “At what?” “Being honest. You do it like a bad accent.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative storytelling within the romance genre. The author successfully establishes the Welsh setting through subtle details like "Cwm Bookshop" and references to Welsh nature writing, while avoiding heavy-handed exposition. The premise of a celebrity hiding from paparazzi in a bookstore is handled with originality, particularly through the unexpected discovery of the model railway in the back room. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices for each character. Elin's dry, practical Welsh sensibility contrasts well with Rhys's initially performative charm that gradually gives way to genuine vulnerability. Lines like "We don't serve celebrity" and "Regret? You keep regret in stock too?" / "It's seasonal" showcase wit and character efficiently. The character development is particularly strong. Rhys is portrayed as the requested "rogue with a fragile ego" - his charm offensive faltering against Elin's immunity creates believable romantic tension. His vulnerability about needing to be liked feels earned rather than manipulative. Elin's internal conflict between surface resistance and growing attraction is well-handled, shown through her physical reactions and increasingly engaged responses. The model railway serves as an excellent plot device, revealing unexpected depth in Rhys while providing a metaphor for his desire to create "small things that don't need me to perform for them." This moment of genuine connection feels organic rather than contrived. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with evocative imagery like "rain found the window" and "something warm and inconvenient move behind her ribs." The pacing builds naturally from initial antagonism to tentative connection. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The ending feels slightly abrupt, and Elin's final line about Rhys doing honesty "like a bad accent" seems somewhat harsh given the genuine moment they've just shared. Some transitions between dialogue exchanges could be smoother, and occasionally the wit feels slightly forced rather than natural. The emotional complexity is well-developed, showing both characters' internal conflicts and the gradual shift in their dynamic. The chemistry builds believably through shared interests and moments of unexpected vulnerability rather than mere physical attraction. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The underhold breathed cold. Aya's fingers found the iron ring and the brass key bit into her palm. Beyond the threshold, the stairwell was a throat of black stone, slick with brine and whale oil. The air tasted of copper, tar, and something older. She stepped inside. Katra followed, coat buttoned to the throat, eyes moving along the walls. Simeon came last, hand on his pistol, the other pressed flat against his waistcoat. There, the pocket watch ticked. Tick. Tick. Tick. Too loud for the silence. "The vault is here," Aya whispered. "Under the old chapel." "No," said a voice from the dark. It was a woman's voice, low and amused, like a blade drawn from a sheath. "Ah. The little aristocrat who plays at thieves." Aya's breath stopped. From the shadows behind the altar emerged a woman in a long oiled leather coat, half lit by a whale oil lamp. Older than Aya, grey haired, scarred over one eyebrow, eyes the flat grey of harbor water. She held a revolver and a key of black iron. Behind her stood six armed Morska bodyguards. Magda Voss. The guild leader. The woman taken in chains only hours before, dragged through the streets in a police wagon. Aya's mind raced. A trap. The arrest had been a lure. They had been walking into it for days. "You are dead," Katra said quietly. "I am decidedly the opposite," Magda replied. Simeon's pistol came up, but he did not fire. "Voss. The raid." "The raid was real enough," Magda said. "They took a body. They took a coat and a hat. The real Magda Voss was in the cellar, watching the tide come in." The pocket watch ticked. Tick. Tick. Tick. Aya's mask was still on. Pale leather and brass, shaped like a fish skull. It had kept her face safe. Now it felt like a cage. "Step away from the altar," Katra said. "Step away from the altar," Magda repeated. "You believe that if you say a thing loudly enough, the world will obey." Katra's hand moved to the knife at her belt. Simeon's hand moved to the watch. The six bodyguards shifted. Their boots on wet stone were the only sound left. Aya lifted her hand. "Wait." Magda looked at her. Aya's voice was steady, though her heart was not. "You know why I am here. You know what I can do. You have always known." Magda's eyes narrowed. "I know what you are. I know what your mother was. I know what you carry in your blood." "I am a useful thing," Aya said. "A key. A door you do not know how to open. Kill me, and you lose the only person in this city who can read the Scythian wards without dying." Simeon said, "Aya." "Shut up, Simeon." Magda smiled. "You think this is a negotiation?" "I think it is arithmetic," Aya said. "You need the artifact. You need me. If I die, you start over with a corpse and a riddle. If I live, I can get you what you want." "The artifact is already mine," Magda said. "I merely needed to see who would come for it. And you did. All three." Katra's jaw tightened. "Expected us?" "Expected you," Magda said, looking at Aya. "The others were only the price you paid to get here." Aya felt the cold move through her. She had thought she was the hunter. But Magda had been playing a longer game, a colder game, and Aya was not a player but a piece. The bodyguards stepped forward. Katra moved first, not to attack, but to put herself between Aya and the men, knife out, face set. "Back off," Katra said. "Katra," Aya said. "Don't." "Back off," Katra said again. Magda raised her revolver, not at Katra, but at the air between them. "You are all under arrest. Treason is punished. Theft of the guild's heart is punished. The use of immateria magick is punished most of all." Aya's mask was removed by a bodyguard. The leather peeled from her face, and the cold air hit her skin. She felt exposed, as if the dark inside her had no place to hide. Magda looked at her face for a long moment. "Aya Vane," she said. "Daughter of Elara Vane. Hanged for the crime of opening a door she should have left shut." "I am not my mother," Aya said. "No," Magda agreed. "You are worse. You are smarter. You have learned to hide it behind a mask and a name. But you are still a Vane. And Vanes always open the wrong door." Simeon's watch ticked. Tick. Tick. Tick. Aya looked at him. His eyes were wide, his hand still on the watch, as if he could stop time by pressing hard enough. "Simeon," she said softly. "Run." He did not move. "Run," she said again. "Now." "I am not leaving you," he said. "You are not a fool," she said. "Run." Magda laughed. "You still think you have choices, child?" Aya looked at the altar. Behind it, in a case of black glass, the Scythian artifact waited. It was a thing of bone and iron, shaped like a whale's tooth, pulsing with a light that was not quite light. The color of a bruise. The color of a lie. "I do not think I have choices," Aya said. "I think I have value. And I am going to use it." Magda lowered her revolver. "Then you had better start using it well." The bodyguards moved in. Katra's knife clattered to the floor. Simeon's pistol was taken from his hand. Aya's arms were twisted behind her back, and the cold iron bit into her wrists. As they were led toward the altar, Aya looked back at the dark. The underhold breathed cold. The pocket watch ticked. Tick. Tick. Tick. And somewhere, in the vast black space between the world and the immateria, something old opened its patient ancient hungry eyes at last.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric world-building within the whalepunk fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a Victorian gothic atmosphere through careful word choice ("whale oil," "brass," "oiled leather coat") and maintains consistent third-person past tense narration with effective internal monologue integration. The dialogue feels authentic to the setting, with characters speaking in measured, formal tones that suit the gritty Victorian aesthetic. Magda Voss emerges as a particularly compelling antagonist with memorable lines like "I am decidedly the opposite" and her cold assessment of Aya as "worse" than her mother. The power dynamics are well-established through dialogue rather than exposition. The scene structure adheres closely to the prompt requirements, hitting all specified story beats: the trio's entry, the confrontation with the supposedly imprisoned guild leader, Aya's unmasking and capture, and her attempt to negotiate based on her value. The revelation that Magda orchestrated the fake arrest creates genuine surprise while remaining logically consistent. Character actions feel believable throughout. Aya's attempt to leverage her magical abilities and aristocratic status as bargaining chips makes tactical sense, while Katra's protective instincts and Simeon's loyalty ring true to established relationships. Magda's patient manipulation demonstrates sophisticated villainy. The prose maintains elegance without becoming overwrought. Phrases like "The underhold breathed cold" and "a throat of black stone" create vivid imagery without excessive ornamentation. The recurring motif of Simeon's pocket watch ("Tick. Tick. Tick.") effectively builds tension. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the "fake arrest" twist, while well-executed, follows familiar patterns. The piece also relies heavily on dialogue to advance plot, which works but occasionally makes the pacing feel static during the standoff. The ending successfully establishes darker implications without feeling forced, particularly the ominous final image of something ancient awakening in the immateria. This feels earned given the established magical elements and gothic tone. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 76.2
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bar smells like spilled beer, burnt sugar, and bad decisions. Spike Spiegel slides onto a cracked vinyl stool, coat open, cigarette already between his lips. The neon sign outside buzzes through the window, painting his face in red. He orders whiskey, pays with coins that have been polished by too many pockets, and watches the door. Revy walks in like the door owes her money. Black crop top, shorts so short they could be called a rumor, a dragon coiled up her right arm. Two pistols hang at her hips, and her eyes find Spike before she reaches the bar. Her smile is all teeth. "You're late," she says. "Traffic." "Traffic doesn't stop for the dead." Spike flicks his lighter. A ring of rust on Spike’s lighter suggests it’s been dropped in water more than once. The flame catches, orange and thin, and he lights the cigarette with a lazy exhale. "Maybe I'm already dead," he says. "Just here for the paperwork." Revy snorts. She orders two whiskeys, drinks one in half, and drops a cigarette in the ashtray with the confidence of someone who has survived worse than bad service. They are hired for the same bounty: a smuggler named Kade, who runs guns through the docks and has a habit of disappearing into the walls of this city. The client does not care who brings him in, alive or otherwise. The body. Kade comes in ten minutes later with two men, both carrying enough muscle to break a window and enough fear to show in their eyes. Spike stands. Revy stands. Their hands move at the same time. The first shot cracks the ceiling. The second sends a bottle exploding against the wall. Spike ducks behind the bar, rolls, and fires twice through the gap in the bottles. One bullet takes Kade's left man in the shoulder. The other punches a hole through a mirror. Revy moves like water around glass. She drops to one knee behind an overturned table, fires left, then right, then left again. Her shots are fast, ugly, and exact. The second man stumbles, spins, and falls with a look of surprise, as if death has arrived wearing a bad attitude. Kade runs for the back door. Spike and Revy both see it. They both move. Outside, the alley is wet with rain and old grease. Kade fires a shotgun from a doorway. Spike rolls under the blast, comes up, and fires three shots. The first two miss. The third catches Kade in the arm. Kade drops the shotgun and runs. Revy catches him against a dumpster, both pistols pressed to his chest. "Stay down," she says. Spike steps up behind her, gun still warm. "You got him," Revy says. "I got him first." "You're breathing through your nose. That means you're thinking." "I'm always thinking." "About what?" "Whether you're going to shoot him or shoot me." Revy laughs. It's not a nice laugh, but it's real. Kade is zip-tied with a length of chain from the dumpster. Spike tosses Revy a cigarette. She takes it without looking, and for a second their fingers touch. Neither of them moves away quickly enough. They walk back to the bar through the rain. Kade is dragged between them, cursing in a language neither of them wants to understand. The bar owner counts his money twice, then slides the bounty envelope across the counter. It is not enough to matter, but it is enough to buy a bottle and a room with a lock that only pretends to work. Revy opens the bottle before they leave. Spike drinks from the neck, then hands it back. Their fingers brush again. This time, neither of them pretends not to notice. The envelope is warm in Spike's pocket, and the bottle is warm in Revy's hand, and neither says it. The motel room is one of those places where the carpet has given up and the ice machine sounds like it's dying. They sit on opposite ends of the bed, still armed, still wet, still trying to decide whether the other one is a threat or a problem. Revy pours two glasses from a bottle she buys at the corner store. She hands Spike one. He takes it. Their eyes meet over the glass. "You're not bad looking," she says. "You're not bad at drinking." "High praise." Spike drinks. The whiskey burns in a way that feels honest. Revy leans back against the wall, boots on the bed, and watches him. "You work alone?" "Mostly." "Good. Alone people are easier to kill." "And you?" "I like company. As long as it doesn't talk too much." Spike smiles. "I'm a professional." "You're a joke with a gun." "Better than a gun with a joke." Revy throws a glass at him. He catches it. She throws another. He catches that too. "Stop it," she says, but she's smiling. Spike sets the glasses on the nightstand. The room is too small. The air is too close. There is a cigarette on the window ledge, and a shadow behind Revy's shoulder that might be a gun, might be a memory, might be the part of her that has learned that softness gets you killed. "You're going to shoot me," Revy says. "Maybe." "Why?" "Because you're good." "Good at what?" "Surviving." Revy steps closer. Spike does not step back. That surprises him. She stops an inch away, close enough that he can smell smoke and cheap soap and the copper edge of her skin. Her eyes are hard, but something under them is not. "Last chance," she says. Spike looks at her mouth. He looks at her guns. He looks at the rust ring on his lighter in his hand, the little scar on metal that remembers water. "Whatever happens," he says, "happens." Revy's hand rises. Spike's does too. Neither of them fires. Neither of them touches. The room holds its breath, and the night waits to see which one of them blinks first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric writing while capturing the essence of both characters effectively. The author successfully creates a noir-tinged encounter that feels authentic to both source materials, with Spike's fatalistic cool and Revy's volatile aggression rendered convincingly. The story structure is solid, moving from initial meeting through action sequence to intimate standoff. The bar shootout is well-choreographed, showing both characters' combat skills without feeling gratuitous. The prose maintains a consistent hardboiled tone throughout, with economical dialogue that captures each character's voice distinctly. Character portrayal is largely successful. Spike's laconic fatalism comes through in lines like "Maybe I'm already dead" and his signature "Whatever happens, happens." Revy's crude directness and underlying vulnerability are present, though perhaps not as fully developed as they could be. Both characters maintain their essential traits while showing subtle attraction and wariness. The imagery is evocative without being overwrought - "walks in like the door owes her money" and "cigarette already between his lips" establish character and atmosphere efficiently. The motel room tension builds effectively, creating genuine sexual tension without resolution. However, some elements feel underdeveloped. The bounty hunt feels somewhat perfunctory - more setup than meaningful plot. Some dialogue exchanges, while stylistically appropriate, border on cliché ("You're not bad looking" / "You're not bad at drinking"). The ending, while thematically appropriate, may leave readers wanting more concrete resolution. The piece occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in character descriptions. Some transitions feel abrupt, and certain metaphors ("moves like water around glass") strain slightly. The pacing is generally good but rushes through some potentially rich moments. Overall, this is competent genre fiction that successfully captures the requested tone and character dynamics, though it doesn't transcend its influences to become truly memorable.
