+ First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 75.9
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The projector squeaks whenever Mr. Patel flips through slides. The slide says “Group Project: Ecosystems,” and my stomach does a tiny flip, because next to the word Group is the name I have been mentally circling for three weeks: Leo. I am not supposed to be nervous. I am in eighth grade, not first. I know what an ecosystem is. I know that a producer converts sunlight into energy, that a decomposer recycles matter, and that a food web has backup options. I know all of this, and I am sitting here with my cold pen held like a weapon. He is already unpacking a notebook. It has a blue cover with a faded comet sticker on the back. I do not know why I noticed the comet. I noticed it because I noticed him, and noticing him is a problem I have not solved. He slides into the desk across from me and says, “Hey,” and I know I should say, “Hey, Leo, I’m excited to work together,” but what comes out is, “Hi,” and it is flat, and it sounds like a door closing. Inside, I am already editing the tape. You were too short. It sounds scared. “Do you want to be the producer?” he asks. My brain offers five answers. One: Yes, I’d love to. Two: I was actually going to take decomposers because I know more about fungi. Three: Does it matter? Four: I don’t mind either way. Five: I’m fine, you choose. I choose five because it is safe, and then I hate myself for choosing five. Five sounds lazy. Five sounds like I don’t care. Five sounds like I am saving my energy for something more important than his opinion of me, which is the exact opposite of true. Again. The projector squeaks. The projector squeaks. Slide two: “Divide responsibilities.” My shoulders rise toward my ears. I lower them. I lower them because I am not sure they lowered. “Maybe we can split it,” he says. “You do the research, I’ll do the slides?” No. No, no, no. If I do all the research, I will be the smart one, and if I am the smart one, he will either think I am trying too hard or think I am better than him, and if I am better than him, he will be polite in a way that is worse than ignoring me. “Actually,” I say, “I was thinking we could both do a little of both.” Good. That is fair. That is cooperative. That is not desperate. Wait. Was that too eager? Did I lean forward? I did lean forward. I always lean forward when I want to disappear. I look down at the table and see my notebook, open to a page where I wrote “ecosystem” five times in different fonts, as if handwriting could make the word less terrifying. He says, “That works,” and his voice is calm, and I want to crawl inside the calm and stay there finally. I begin to rehearse the next conversation. When we pass the lab materials, I will say, “Nice binder.” No. Too flirty. “I like your binder.” Too direct. “Is that a comet?” Too nerdy. “Do you like space?” Too broad. “Your binder is very organized.” Too teacher. “I noticed your binder.” Too creepy. I have been in this classroom for four minutes and I have already produced a binder conversation that would make a novelist blush. He passes me a marker. Our fingers do not touch. I am disappointed, which is absolutely unacceptable. I am not a movie character. Still close. But when he says, “Here,” I want to say, “Thank you, Leo, your hand is close to mine.” Instead I say, “Thanks,” and my voice goes up like a question, and now I sound like I am asking if I am allowed to exist. The projector squeaks. Slide three: “Choose your organism.” I have chosen a fungus. I chose it before I knew I would be paired with him, which means I am not doing it to impress him, which means I should be relieved, but I am still not relieved because I have to explain why fungi are cool. “Fungi are cool,” I say. He looks at me. “Yeah?” Yes. Yes, they are cool. They connect trees underground. They trade nutrients. Some help plants survive drought. They are the internet of the forest. I could say that. I could say, “They’re like a hidden network,” and he would look interested, and then I could say, “I read about it,” and he would ask what I read, and then I would have to tell him about the article I read while pretending to be asleep, and then he would think I am weird, and confirmed weird is a permanent address. I monitor my face. Are my eyebrows up? Are my eyes too wide? Is my mouth doing the little tight thing I do when I am trying not to smile? I smile now, just a little, to prove I am not a monster. The smile feels painted on, like a sticker. He does not seem to notice. That is better. If he notices, I will have to explain that I am practicing social skills, and that is not a sentence a normal eighth-grader says unless she is in a therapy commercial. You blinked too slowly. Legs crossed wrong. Close. Still. The classroom is full of other pairs talking about volcanoes, coral reefs, wolves, and I am sitting here with a comet notebook and a fungus. He asks, “Do you want to meet after school to start the outline?” My heart makes a sound that is not in the science textbook. I can say yes. I can say yes and be normal. I can say yes and not analyze the word outline until it loses meaning. I open my mouth. The projector squeaks. I close it. “I’ll check my schedule,” I say. Two weeks is enough time, maybe. I wait. Still.

The structure effectively mirrors the protagonist's mental state - fragmented, repetitive, and circular, much like anxious thought patterns. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Sixteen percent. My thumb hovers over the screen, watching the number sit there like a small wound. I tell myself I’m just checking the time, but I’m checking the exit, the way out, the evidence. If he can’t be reached, he’s with someone else. If he replies too quickly, he’s bored. If he doesn’t reply, I already know what I’ll say: you don’t have to come tonight, I don’t want to be the person who needs you. My voice in my head sounds sweet, wounded, perfect. It has always been more persuasive than the real one, every single time, now. He texts: Hey, are you still up? Four words. I reread them until the letters blur. Are you still up means I’m waiting for you to perform. Are you still up means I’m checking if you’ve finally become manageable. I type, I’m here, then delete it. Too available. I type, Yes, then delete it. Too eager. I type, I’m getting ready, but my stomach tightens. If I’m getting ready, I’m making a production. If I’m not, I’m not trying. He must be deciding whether I’m worth the drive. I can hear him say, You’re so intense, in a soft voice. He sends another text before I answer: I picked up the coffee you like. My heart slams. For one second, I am the person who was remembered. The warmth is so sudden it feels like a bruise. Then I think, Why did you mention it? You’re reminding me you’re generous. You’re reminding me I’m the one who needs. I imagine him holding the cup, watching the steam, smiling with the patience of someone who has already decided I’m a problem. I imagine myself saying, You didn’t have to, and meaning, You shouldn’t have, because kindness is a debt every time. I stand in front of the mirror and practice my face. Calm. Light. I touch my jaw as if I can loosen the tension there. If he says you’ve been distant, I’ll say I’ve been busy, which is true and not true. If he says you’re always like this, I’ll laugh and say I’m dramatic, which will make it worse. If he says I need space, I’ll say of course, and I’ll feel the world crack. I keep the phone in my hand like a lifeline, though the battery is now fifteen percent. I need to hear his voice now. His car lights sweep across my window. I freeze. He didn’t say he was coming, so this is a test. Or he’s been waiting and is tired. I pick up the phone and the screen dies, then blinks back at fourteen percent. I almost call him, but what if he’s already decided I’m too much? Then I hear his knock, low and careful, and my body answers before my mind does. I open the door. He’s holding the coffee. He says, Hi, you made it, and his eyes find mine with a softness I don’t really deserve at all. He steps inside and says, I missed you. I wanted that. I wanted it badly. My chest opens, and for a moment I am not performing, not rehearsing, just held. Then the thought arrives: he said it because I looked ready to collapse. He’s managing me. I ask, Did you mean it? He frowns. Of course I meant it. I nod, but I’m already building the case. He meant it then. He can stop meaning it by tomorrow. I can feel the love in the room, warm and real, and I can’t stop testing its edges again and again, always. He sets the coffee on the table and says, gently, You’re safe here. The words land softly like a hand on my shoulder. I want to believe them so badly. I believe them, really. I hate that I believe them, because if I let myself, I’ll be vulnerable, and vulnerability is the door where he gets in. I think, This is the pattern. I know the pattern. I also know knowing it isn’t the same as stopping it. My mouth opens. I say, Thank you, but my voice sounds like it belongs to someone braver than I am still tonight. He sits close enough that I can smell the coffee on his dark jacket. He says, quietly, I’m not going anywhere. The sentence is simple. It is also a rope. I grab it, then I cut it. He must mean it for tonight. He must mean it until I prove I’m inconvenient. I watch his hands. They’re steady. I want to say, Stay, but I say, You don’t have to. He looks at me, patient and tired, and I see the version of him I’ve made: the one who is already leaving, only not yet, not now, not soon, maybe. Later, he touches my wrist and says, I like you. Not love, yet, but like, which is a door. I almost collapse into it. I need it so much it hurts. Then I think, He’s saying it because I’m easy to feel sorry for. He’s saying it because he’s lonely. I ask, Do you like me enough? He laughs, a real laugh, and says, Enough to be here. For a second, I believe him. For a second, the room stops spinning. Then I wonder if the laugh was pity, and I hate that I need to know it now again. His phone buzzes. He glances at it and says, I’ll call you tomorrow. The offer is warm. It is also a promise I will sabotage. I say, You don’t have to, and immediately want to take the words back. He squeezes my hand. I feel the life in his grip, real and temporary. My phone dies in my pocket, black and final. Maybe that’s a mercy. I don’t have to watch the clock, don’t have to count the hours, don’t have to hear my own mind turn his kindness into evidence against me, as if it were true, always now.

+ Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 68.2
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Blood Debt The torch in its iron bracket on the eastern wall had burned down to a stub of blackened tallow, and its flame was the only thing moving in the temple besides the two men it lit. The hall had lost its roof long ago; broken pillars stood like ribs, and the floor was a mosaic of cracked flagstones, moss, and old blood. Outside the ruined south door, rain hissed against the night. Inside, the crowd had pressed against the rubble in two uneven bands: Jigen-ryū disciples in dark hakama to the west, Piguaquan fighters in patched jackets to the east, their voices low and hungry. Coins changed hands in the dark. No one spoke of the masters’ orders. No one needed to. Kaito stood at the southern end of the clearing, three paces from the broken threshold where the south door had fallen inward. His feet were parallel, knees sunk, weight low in his heels. He wore the old Jigen-ryū cut, a short jacket buttoned to the throat, and his face had the flat, proud stillness of a blade before it was drawn. Across the stone platform, seven paces north, Lin waited by the collapsed altar. His stance was narrower, feet angled, toes pressing into the cracks as if the floor might open. His jacket was ragged at the hem, his knuckles white, his eyes bright with an anger that had no place in a temple. Neither moved first. The torch snapped. A shadow leapt from Kaito’s shoulder and struck the western wall, then snapped back. Lin shifted his weight to the ball of his left foot. Kaito’s right heel lifted a hair. The crowd leaned in, breath held, coins forgotten in cupped hands. The rivalry between their schools had outlived the men who started it: Jigen-ryū, born in elite houses, said Piguaquan was street noise, a brawl dressed as technique. Piguaquan, raised in docks, kitchens, and guardhouses, said Jigen-ryū was a dead man’s pride, all posture and no survival. Tonight, in this rotting temple, both insults were about to be tested with bone and breath. Kaito broke stillness. He drove forward in a straight line, right fist leading in a short, brutal thrust toward Lin’s throat, left fist chambered at his hip. The Jigen-ryū step was explosive, his body compressing like a bowstring before releasing. Lin did not meet the thrust. He pivoted on his left foot, stepped to his left—toward the torch—and let Kaito’s right hand pass the west side of his jaw. In the same motion, Lin’s right arm whipped around, elbow bent, palm turning under, and cracked into Kaito’s right shoulder. The blow was not heavy, but it landed on a tendon. Kaito’s shoulder jerked. His forward momentum carried him a half-step west, off the central line, into shadow. Kaito recovered with a sharp pivot on his left foot, turning the stagger into a cut to the east. His right elbow came up to protect his neck, and his left foot swept across the stone, closing the distance. He was faster than Lin expected. A hammer blow descended toward the top of Lin’s skull. Lin dropped his center, let the hammer pass over his left shoulder, and sprang south around Kaito’s right side. His left foot found a crack in the flagstone; he used the slip as a pivot and threw a low, circular kick at Kaito’s lead leg. The kick missed the ankle by a hand’s width, but the sound of it made the western crowd hiss. Lin was already moving north again, but Kaito was not finished. He caught the inside of Lin’s right wrist with his left hand and used the grip to yank Lin forward. The Piguaquan fighter’s feet scrambled on the wet stone. Kaito drove his right palm into Lin’s solar plexus, a short, driving blow that folded Lin’s breath. Lin’s back struck the base of the collapsed altar, two paces north of where he had started. For one instant, he was pinned, the altar stone hard against his shoulder blades, Kaito’s weight pressing in from the southwest. The torch flickered, and the shadows of both men stretched long and thin against the broken wall behind Lin. Kaito raised his right fist for a finishing blow. Lin saw the shoulder rise and did the only thing Piguaquan had taught him for this: he did not block. He rolled his left shoulder under the fist, twisted his hips to the east, and stepped around Kaito’s right side with a small, circling movement. The altar gave him no room, but the cracked stone gave him a handhold. He grabbed a splinter of wood from the altar’s edge, used it to anchor his body, and snapped his right arm across in a whipping arc. The palm struck Kaito’s left temple just as Kaito’s fist passed over Lin’s head. The sound was wet and flat. Kaito’s eyes rolled. His legs buckled. He fell west, his shoulder striking shadowed stone, not the flame, and the torch swung in its bracket, throwing a brief red smear across the wall. Lin stood over him, chest heaving, right hand trembling. Kaito lay on his side, one eye shut, blood threading from his nose into the dark. The crowd did not cheer. The Jigen-ryū disciples on the west went rigid; the Piguaquan fighters on the east exhaled as if a debt had been paid. Lin looked down, not with triumph but with the tired clarity of a man who had known the strike might kill. He stepped back, placing his feet apart again, and waited. Kaito moved, slowly, rolling onto his knees. The torch guttered low again. In the ruins, the old hatred had not ended; it had only found a new scar to remember by. Somewhere in the dark, a cold coin slipped from a hand and rang once on stone, but no one moved to retrieve it. The temple held its breath, waiting for the next wound. The night was not done yet. It waited still.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution in several key areas while falling short in others. The author successfully maintains the requested physical coherence throughout the fight sequence, clearly tracking both fighters' positions relative to each other and the temple environment. The spatial dynamics are precise - we can visualize Kaito's initial position by the south door, Lin's placement by the collapsed altar, and their movements throughout the encounter. The atmospheric writing is particularly effective. The crumbling temple setting is vividly rendered with concrete details like the guttering torch, broken flagstones, and collapsed altar. The author skillfully uses these environmental elements as active components in the fight choreography rather than mere backdrop. The fight mechanics themselves are well-crafted and believable. Each strike, counter, and movement follows logically from the established martial arts styles. Kaito's explosive, linear Jigen-ryū attacks contrast effectively with Lin's circular, evasive Piguaquan responses. The final sequence where Lin uses the altar as leverage for his decisive strike is particularly well-executed. However, the piece suffers from significant character development weaknesses. Both fighters remain essentially blank slates defined only by their fighting styles and social backgrounds. We learn nothing meaningful about their individual personalities, motivations beyond generic pride, or what specifically drives their personal animosity. The "generations-old rivalry" feels like exposition rather than lived tension. The prose occasionally veers toward overwrought territory with phrases like "the old hatred had not ended; it had only found a new scar to remember by" and the repetitive ending structure. Some descriptions, while atmospheric, border on purple prose without adding substantial meaning. The pacing is generally strong, building tension effectively before the confrontation and maintaining momentum throughout the fight. The crowd's presence adds appropriate stakes and atmosphere without becoming distracting. The ending feels somewhat anticlimactic and artificially extended. The fight concludes decisively, but the author seems reluctant to end, adding several unnecessary final paragraphs that diminish rather than enhance the impact. + Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 65.7
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The digital clock glows fourteen minutes fifty-nine seconds above mirrors. Eighteen of us stand in a three-by-six grid, two meters apart, facing downstage. I am back row, third from the left, behind Joon. My cheap sneakers press into marley floor. Famous Maester Han breaks students to remake them. He stands downstage center, arms crossed, white jacket sharp. He does not count. He claps once. His eyes find me. I feel my scholarship shrink in my tiny, small, cheap pocket now. He calls the K-pop phrase. Right hand crosses over left, palm out, left foot steps to second position, knees bend. Then torso pivots right, right foot slides to fifth, arms open wide, head snaps left. Eight counts, clean exact lines. My body hears the rhythm before my mind does. My hips want to roll, my shoulders want to shim, my feet want to boogie. I lock them behind the grid. All the other trainees move like polished cold bright steel. On count one, I cross my right hand over my left, palm flat, fingers pointing downstage. My left foot slides into second position, heel lifting, knee bending. The movement is foreign, stiff, and my spine straightens against the hard beat. On count five, I pivot right, my right foot sliding to fifth position, toes pointed, weight shifting. Both arms open to second position, elbows high. My head snaps left, but my neck twitches too loose, a tiny street tell again. Maester Han stops the track. His clap cracks. He walks upstage, past the first row, past the second, until he stands directly in front of me. The clock reads twelve minutes, red, patient, watching us from the wall above all. His voice is low. No flavor. No street. We are a machine. I swallow. My throat tastes like dust from the concrete courts where I first learned to move and the smell of rain that never comes here in Seoul. He starts the track again. We reset to the grid. I face downstage, arms at my sides, feet parallel, weight centered. Joon’s back is smooth, a wall of discipline while my shoulders tremble with every downbeat I count silently now. Count one: right hand crosses, palm out. Count two: left foot steps. Count three: knees sink. Count four: hold. Count five: pivot right. Count six: slide to fifth. Count seven: arms open. Count eight: snap. My chest pops too early. The pop is a betrayal. It is the move I made at block parties, a sudden hit in the ribs to make the crowd lean in. Here, it ruins the line and makes me small in his eyes again now. The clock drops to nine minutes. We run the phrase twice more. On the second run, my left foot drags a tiny shuffle, a street step I cannot erase. My heel catches the marley and pulls me off beat now. Han freezes us. He points at my foot. Your heel is lying, he says. Your feet are from the street, not from this room. I look down at my cheap sneakers and feel the floor judging each step I hold. The words land like a slap. I think of my mother, counting bus fare, and my cousin laughing as I froze on a curb. I am not here to be polished into someone else. I want to stay myself here. But the scholarship is also a bridge. If I leave now, I return to cracked pavement, to dances that end when the police whistle. I want more, but I fear losing the voice that made me who I am still. The clock reads six minutes. Han resets us. This time, he asks for the final eight counts with a personal mark. He points at me. Show me what you are. I stand in back row, third from left, and wait. The track starts. The first four counts are the same: cross, step, bend, hold. The room tightens. My neighbors freeze in perfect unison, their arms forming clean diagonal lines while I balance on my heels afraid to break the shape. Count five: pivot right. My hip tries to roll, a lazy street circle. I stop it with a sharp chest isolation, forcing my torso to turn as a single block. My spine stays vertical and my head snaps left now. Count six: slide to fifth. My right foot extends, toe pointed, heel high. Count seven: arms open. I feel the air pull at my sleeves, clean and commercial, not wild, but my wrists itch for a lock, a freeze now. Count eight is the decision. The choreography says snap left, hold. My body wants to pop, to lock, to break. If I add flavor, I become myself. If I obey, I become theirs. The clock flashes three minutes and waits. I choose both. I snap left, but inside the snap I let one small pop live in my chest, no larger than a heartbeat. My arms open, then close around the hidden beat. My foot stays in fifth position clean. The final pose is a diagonal line from my back left heel to my front right toe. My chest is still, but my ribs remember the block party. I have not broken formation. I have kept a door inside me. Han walks to my mark. He stops two meters away, directly downstage, and looks at the mirror. His jaw tightens. He sees the pop, but he also sees the line. The clock reads one minute and his eyes find me. He does not praise me. He claps once, sharp as a whip. Again, he says, but faster. The command is a threat and a promise. I reset my feet to parallel. My hands open at sides and I breathe now. The clock counts zero, but the track does not stop. I move into the next eight, my body a machine with a hidden street heart, precise and alive, still mine. In Seoul, I am learning to break and to stay.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution in several key areas while falling short in others. The author successfully maintains the required physical coherence throughout, tracking spatial relationships with precision - the narrator's position "back row, third from left, behind Joon" and the detailed choreography descriptions create a clear visual map. The kinetic descriptions effectively contrast street dance fluidity with K-pop precision through specific technical language and body positioning. The cultural and class tensions are well-established through concrete details like "cheap sneakers" and references to the narrator's mother counting bus fare. The internal conflict between authenticity and conformity builds naturally to the climactic decision point where the protagonist chooses to hide a small "pop" within the prescribed choreography - a nuanced resolution that avoids easy answers. However, the prose suffers from significant structural and stylistic issues. The writing frequently fragments into choppy, incomplete sentences that disrupt flow: "I feel my scholarship shrink in my tiny, small, cheap pocket now." The repetitive use of "now" as a sentence ender becomes distracting. Some descriptions veer toward overwrought territory: "my throat tastes like dust from the concrete courts where I first learned to move and the smell of rain that never comes here in Seoul." The character voice, while attempting to capture the narrator's outsider status, sometimes feels artificially constructed rather than authentic. The emotional complexity is present but could be more deeply explored - the protagonist's internal struggle feels somewhat surface-level despite the rich setup. The piece succeeds in avoiding unearned transformations and maintains appropriate tonal darkness throughout. The ending strikes the right balance between hope and uncertainty. The technical dance terminology effectively highlights the collision between styles, and the physical descriptions generally achieve the required vividness. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bench is a shelf of compressed sighs. The clerk shuffles papers that smell of forgotten Tuesdays. Dream sits at its center, his face, typically impenetrable, betraying a quiet sense of irritation. "Case 77,104.1," he says. "Territorial dispute in the recurring dream of Max Alder, age fourteen. First Love versus Mora, the Sleep-Weight." First Love rises. She is small, rosy-cheeked, and clutches a folder of heartbeats. First Love's cheeks redden, which is legally significant in the Dreaming. "Your Somnium," she begins, "the dream is crafted with care. A field of wildflowers. A boy lying on his back. A girl beside him. They talk. They laugh. They almost kiss. The emotion is muddled, warm, and unresolved. It is a first love." "It is also a feeding ground," says Mora. She sits on the defendant's side, a thin grey shape who has learned to be heavy. Her cackles are faint, but they echo uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings. "Objection," says First Love. "To the implication." "None," says Dream. "I meant objection to the implication that my work is a feeding ground." "Objection noted," Dream says. "Denied." Max Alder appears in the witness box in one sock and a look of regret. Max's sock twitches again. "Mr. Alder," First Love says, "did you experience the dream as comfort?" "Yes." "Did you find Lily agreeable?" "She is... nice." "And after the incident?" Max swallows. "The flowers smell like metal." Mora leans forward. "I prefer 'ozone and ripe fear,' but go on." "Describe the deviation," Dream says. First Love produces a glass vial. Inside, a tiny field turns. A girl climbs onto the boy, laughing, and the sky curdles. Her face stretches into something tall, dark, and faintly beautiful. She settles on his chest, and drinks his breath in white threads. The court goes quiet. A minor dream of a wedding cake in the gallery begins to apologize to itself. "That is not what I made," First Love whispers. "That is what he wanted," Mora says. "Deep down. You just didn't have the nerve." "I have the nerve," First Love says, offended. "I simply do not make nightmares." "You make near-misses," Mora says. "A near-kiss is a near-death experience for the heart. I merely follow through." "Followed through by suffocating a child?" Dream asks. "By assisting respiration," Mora says. "He is holding his breath. I provide motivation." "Mr. Alder," Dream says, "did you hold your breath?" Max looks at the floor. "I am trying to be cool." "Of course you are." First Love produces a drawing of a heart with a small lock on it. "The dream is based on anticipation. The almost-kiss is the point. Mora's intrusion converts longing into terror. That is vandalism." Mora spreads her hands. Her fingers are slightly too long. "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?" "Which girl?" Dream asks. "The dreamer's crush." "Lily is a fictional construct." "So am I, technically. We're all constructs. But I'm a construct with a metabolism." "You are a Slavic nightmare spirit," says the clerk, a dry little man made of unfinished poems. "And still a girl." Dream rubs his temples. The gesture costs him a mask. For a moment, his face is a field of black grain, and the court flinches. "Order," he says. "I have adjudicated the murder of gods, the theft of a city's sleep, and a dispute over a burning library. I do not expect to be here for a schoolboy's crush and a chest-sitter." Mora smiles. It is a good smile, in the way a knife is a good knife. "The dream is Max's," Dream says. "Your Somnium cannot award ownership to a dreamer," First Love protests. "The question is authorship." "Then the question is authorship." Dream looks at First Love. "You built the field. You built the girl. You built the almost-kiss." "I did." "Mora," he says, "you built the terror." "I built the appetite." Dream stands. The court leans in without leaning. "I find for First Love," he says. "The dream shall be restored. The wildflowers will bloom. Lily will remain Lily. The almost-kiss will remain almost." First Love clutches her folder. "Thank you." "However," Dream continues, "the dreamer has a deficiency in basic respiratory technique. To prevent recurrence, the dream shall include a small grey bird perched on a fence post, reminding Max to breathe. The bird will be unobtrusive, but persistent." Mora's cackles echo again, thinner this time. "And Mora?" First Love asks. Dream looks at her with the patience of a wall. "Mora is appointed Warden of the Threshold between the Dream and the Sleeper's chest. She may sit there only when the dreamer is awake and consented, as a mild pressure, and she shall be provided one cup of cold tea per night, brewed from regret. If she consumes breath again, I will make her dream of being a librarian." Mora blinks. "That's worse than death." "It is worse than boredom," Dream says. "Which is all I have." Max raises his hand. "Can I still have the almost-kiss?" Dream looks at him for a long moment. Then, very slightly, the corner of his mouth moves. It is not a smile. It is a crack in a door. "Yes," he says. "But next time, kiss her before she becomes a problem." The gavel, a thorn from the first nightmare ever told, comes down. Mora emits faint cackles that echo uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings as she is led out by two clerks who would rather be anywhere else, including a coma. First Love gathers her heartbeats. "Your Somnium, that is... generous." Dream is already reviewing the next case: a dispute between a recurring dream of a beach and the actual concept of thirst. "It is not generosity," he says. "It is an experiment." First Love frowns. "An experiment?" Dream's face remains a door. But for the first time in centuries, the door is slightly ajar. "Let us see," he says, "if a boy learns to breathe, or if the girl learns to bite."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully creating a courtroom drama set in Neil Gaiman's Dreaming with the requested dark comedy tone. The author captures Dream's characteristic voice and mannerisms effectively, particularly his growing irritation at having to adjudicate such mundane matters despite his cosmic responsibilities. The dialogue is consistently strong throughout, with each character maintaining a distinct voice. Mora's pragmatic "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" perfectly encapsulates her mercenary nature, while First Love's earnest protests about her craft feel authentic. The exchanges between characters flow naturally and serve both comedic and plot purposes. The world-building is economical but evocative. Details like "a bench of compressed sighs," "papers that smell of forgotten Tuesdays," and "a gavel made from a thorn from the first nightmare ever told" create atmosphere without overwhelming the narrative. The author follows the instruction to use descriptives sparingly while still establishing the fantastical setting. The comedy emerges organically from the absurd situation and character interactions rather than forced jokes. The bureaucratic nature of adjudicating dream disputes, combined with the serious treatment of ridiculous circumstances, creates effective dark humor. Moments like the wedding cake dream apologizing to itself in the gallery demonstrate creative comedic touches. The resolution shows genuine creativity and understanding of Dream's character. Rather than a simple ruling, Dream crafts a solution that serves multiple purposes - restoring the original dream while addressing the underlying issue and providing Mora with alternative sustenance. His final comment about conducting an "experiment" reveals his mischievous nature while maintaining the ambiguous tone appropriate to the character. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with sentences that flow naturally and imagery that serves the story rather than showing off. The author avoids purple prose while still creating memorable phrases and maintaining the slightly archaic, formal tone appropriate to the Dreaming's court proceedings. Character motivations remain believable within the fantastical context. First Love's protective stance toward her creation, Mora's practical hunger, and Dream's weary authority all feel authentic. The minor character of Max, appearing confused and embarrassed, adds human grounding to the supernatural proceedings. The piece maintains narrative coherence throughout, building logically from the initial dispute through testimony to resolution. The pacing allows for both character development and plot advancement without feeling rushed or meandering. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 63.0
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Blood Moon A crimson harvest moon bleeds over the thatched roofs, turning the deserted village into a wound that will not close. Mud, ash, and spilled wine stain the cobblestones. Behind a shuttered chapel, a bell has been silenced by a tongue of iron. The air tastes of iron, lilac, and graves. Alucard walks the street as if he owns the silence. His red coat sways like a banner of war, his wide-brimmed hat tilting against the moonlight, his orange lenses swallowing the pale glow. The village dogs are already dead, their jaws slack, their eyes dull. He is looking for something. A woman stands at the square's edge, arms folded, black dress torn at the hem. Her hair falls in a dark river to her waist. Her violet eyes narrow as if the world has offended her. She smells of lilac and gooseberries, a sweetness that cuts through blood and smoke. Yennefer of Vengerberg watches the red-coated stranger approach and decides, with the cold calm of a woman who has survived courts, armies, betrayal, and her own ambitions, that she will not be the first to speak tonight under the crimson harvest moon, in the ruined village, entirely still alone now. Yennefer lifts her chin, her violet eyes sharpening. “And the night has brought a clown. If you are here to frighten me, you have chosen poorly. I have seen worse than your coat, and I have buried men far more dangerous than your smile tonight, under the moon, I suppose.” Alucard smiles, showing teeth that are too long, too white, too eager. “Worse? How delightfully presumptuous. I am Alucard. The bird of Hermes is my name. I eat my wings to make me tame, though I have never learned how to stop before the dawn breaks, perhaps, tonight, maybe still.” “Poetry,” she says flatly, her voice cutting through the silence. “I despise it. Next.” He laughs, a sound like a blade dragged across bone, slow and wet. “You do not fear me? Most people do, though they rarely admit it before the dark takes them tonight, under the moon, perhaps.” “I fear stupidity,” Yennefer replies. “And I have little patience for monsters who announce themselves before they strike.” Alucard tilts his head. “Monsters? How pedestrian. I am not a monster. I am what happens when a creature refuses to kneel to the moon, sun, God, or men. I am hunger.” She steps closer, her hand drifting to the silver pendant at her throat. “And you pretend to be a man in a ridiculous hat. Your aura is wrong. Too cold. Too old. You smell of centuries. You are no nobleman. You are night-walker, blood-eater, grave-crawler that calls itself old king.” “You are curious,” she says, “the first creature in two hundred years who has not asked me for a favor, a curse, or a crown. That makes you more interesting than the dozen men who tried to buy my silence tonight, perhaps.” He grins. “Then I shall not disappoint you.” Yennefer’s hand snaps forward. The lanterns gutter. The air thickens with the scent of ozone and crushed violets. A circle of silvered runes blooms on the cobblestones beneath Alucard’s feet, spinning into a cage of light. The runes bite at his boots, his coat, the air around him once more. Alucard looks down as if he has noticed a stain on his sleeve. “Cute,” he says. The cage flares. Chains of violet fire leap from the runes and wrap around his wrists, his throat, his shoulders. Yennefer presses her palm against the air and pushes, her face pale with effort. Alucard’s coat splits from shoulder to hem. A gash opens across his chest, revealing black blood and the dark architecture of his wound. He does not fall. He does not gasp. He simply laughs, and the sound fills the square like a promise under the red moon, tonight, perhaps, soon. “You are strong,” he says, and there is genuine admiration in his voice. “I like that. Most women beg. Most men break. You merely try to kill me before dessert.” Yennefer’s violet eyes flash. “I am not sweet, and I am not a maiden in distress in need of saving.” “No,” Alucard says, “you are far more dangerous than that.” He pulls his hands free. The chains shatter like glass. The runes crack and die, leaving scorch marks and the smell of burnt lilac. Alucard’s wound closes in an obscene ripple, the flesh knitting itself together with a wet sound. Yennefer steps back, her expression cold, but her fingers tremble once. She notices it. He notices it. Neither admits it. “Again,” she says, and the square holds its breath as the moonlight bends around them like a blade waiting to fall under the red sky, tonight, perhaps, at last, now. Alucard draws a pistol from beneath his coat. It is absurdly large, black as a coffin, its barrel thick as a man’s arm. He raises it with a lazy elegance and fires. The bullet is silver. It screams through the night and strikes her where the heart should be now. Yennefer does not die. A web of violet light explodes from her chest, catching the bullet midflight, grinding it to dust before it can pierce her skin. The shockwave shatters the windows of the nearest houses. Dust and glass rain down around them in the square, under the moon, tonight. Alucard lowers the gun, delighted. “Ahh. Now we are playing.” Yennefer spits blood, though her lips remain straight. “You are louder than you are smart.” “I am both,” he says. “And you are wounded.” “I am always wounded. It is what makes me useful under the moon, perhaps.” For a moment, their power balances. The air between them bends. The moon turns deeper red. The village holds its breath. Then Yennefer turns and walks away, her steps steady, her chin high. Alucard watches her go, his gun still in hand, his blood still dripping under the red moon.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece attempts an ambitious crossover between two popular fictional universes, setting up an encounter between Alucard from Hellsing and Yennefer from The Witcher. The story succeeds in several areas while struggling with significant technical and stylistic issues. The atmospheric opening is genuinely effective, establishing a gothic mood with vivid imagery of the blood moon and abandoned village. The author demonstrates a solid understanding of both characters' core traits - Alucard's sadistic arrogance and regenerative abilities, Yennefer's pride and magical prowess. The power dynamic shifts as requested, with neither character backing down or showing weakness first. However, the prose suffers from severe structural problems. Repetitive phrases like "under the moon, tonight, perhaps" appear throughout, creating an awkward, almost stammering rhythm that disrupts the flow. These seem like editing artifacts or AI-generated repetitions rather than intentional stylistic choices. The writing occasionally veers into purple prose territory with overwrought descriptions, though it generally maintains atmospheric effectiveness. The dialogue captures both characters' voices reasonably well - Yennefer's cutting sarcasm and Alucard's theatrical menace come through clearly. The famous quotes are incorporated naturally. The magical combat sequence is well-choreographed, showing both characters' abilities without either definitively winning. The story structure works as a character study and initial encounter, building tension through their verbal sparring and brief physical confrontation before Yennefer's strategic withdrawal. This ending feels earned rather than forced, maintaining the requested power balance. Technical issues include some awkward sentence constructions and the persistent repetitive phrases that significantly detract from readability. The piece also occasionally tells rather than shows, particularly in character descriptions, though it generally maintains good show-don't-tell practices during action sequences. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 78.0
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals. The pale buzz is the only sound beyond a cracked pipe's drip. Jolyne Cujoh stands against the cold wall, her two buns tight, her butterfly tattoo peeking from beneath a torn sleeve. She has been in this supernatural prison for three days, and every guard, inmate, and whispering shadow seems to know her name before she speaks it. She does not like it here. The cells are stacked like jars. The food tastes like rust. The prisoners have leashes. Footsteps approach. They are soft, deliberate, and pleasant for a place that smells like wet iron. Makima appears in the light, her auburn hair falling neatly over one shoulder. Her yellow eyes ringed like a dog's collar look over Jolyne with quiet amusement. 'You look uncomfortable,' Makima says. Her voice is honey poured over gravel. 'Most people here stop complaining after the first night.' Jolyne pushes off the wall. 'Who are you? A guard? A warden? Or one of those leashed things that wears a smile?' Makima does not flinch. 'I decide which leashes stay and which get cut. I am Makima. And you, Miss Cujoh, are the interesting new arrival.' 'Interesting.' Jolyne's jaw tightens. 'That's what they say before they try to own something.' Makima tilts her head. 'You have a strange power. I see it moving under your skin like thread. A Stand, yes? The guards called it a string trick. They were not wrong.' Stone Free snaps into existence behind Jolyne. Its strings coil around her arms, ready to tear, slice, or bind. 'You saw it because you looked too long. That's your first mistake.' Makima smiles. 'My second mistake will be assuming you are as smart as your father. He is dead. Are you?' Jolyne's eyes narrow. 'You don't know my father. You don't get to use his name.' 'No,' Makima agrees softly, 'but I know what you want. You want to leave. You want to protect the people you love. You want to prove you are not the murderer. Those are useful things. I can arrange them.' Something cold settles in Jolyne's stomach. 'Arrange them how?' 'By giving me a contract.' Makima steps closer. The light flickers again; the shadows behind her look like collars. 'Answer a few questions. Tell me what you would do to save someone. Then I will know whether you are a dog, a devil, or something worth keeping.' Jolyne's strings vibrate. 'You talk like a cop, but you smell like a cage.' Makima's expression does not change. 'Cops protect. I organize. There is a difference, though the leash is the same. Call me manipulative. I call it order.' 'Order.' Jolyne laughs, sharp and ugly. 'You think people are just animals waiting for a hand to hold them down?' Makima's yellow eyes shine. 'I think animals are easier to understand. And you, Jolyne, have a loud instinct. It tells me you will not listen. That is why I will test you.' Before Jolyne can answer, the lights die. In the dark, Jolyne hears Makima's voice from everywhere at once. 'If I asked you to cut your own hand and give it to me, would you? If I asked you to let a friend die so you could walk out of here, would you? If I told you obedience would save your father's name, would you kneel?' Jolyne's heart pounds, but her breathing stays even. She remembers her father's voice: calm, short, certain. She remembers the friends she has lost, the lies that built this prison, and Makima's smile while asking for blood. 'No,' Jolyne says. The lights return. Makima stands where she is, as if darkness has never touched her. 'No,' Makima repeats. 'That is disappointing, but not surprising. You are not a dog. You are a cat that learned to wear a collar because it thought the collar was a necklace.' Jolyne's strings lash out. One wraps around Makima's throat. Another cuts the leash on a cowering inmate across the hall. The inmate gasps, rubs his neck, and does not look up. Makima does not cough or struggle. She looks at the string around her throat like a child examining a ribbon. 'You think you can control me with a thread?' she asks. 'No,' Jolyne says. 'I think you are finally showing your face.' Makima's smile widens. 'Clever. But clever people still have desires. You want to be free. I want to understand what freedom means when the owner lets the leash go.' Jolyne pulls the string tight. Makima's knees bend, then straighten. The Stand cannot crush her, only bind her. Jolyne finally sees something behind the sweet mask: not fear, but hunger. 'You are not a person here,' Jolyne says. 'You are the cage.' Makima laughs. It is a small, clean sound. 'A cage needs a key. You just made one. If I let you go, will you still think you are free? Or will you wonder who cut the leash? Will you wonder if I saved you to watch you learn?' Jolyne's strings tremble. The question is a trap, but it is also true. Every kindness in this prison has a price. Makima smiles because she is collecting answers. 'If there's no Mickey,' Jolyne says, 'this shit ain't Disney.' Makima's yellow eyes soften. 'Then let us make it a little better. I will give you a chance to leave. In exchange, answer one final question: what would you do if your freedom cost someone else theirs?' Jolyne looks down the corridor. In the flickering light, she sees leashed prisoners, broken guards, and shadows that obey without asking why. She understands now: Makima does not need to force her. Makima only needs to make the choice feel like mercy, not like love. Jolyne unstrings her own hand and throws it at Makima's face. The string explodes into a web, slicing the flickering light, the leash, and the very careful smile. 'Nothing,' Jolyne says. 'I take what I need.'
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong atmospheric writing and character understanding, creating a tense psychological confrontation between two well-realized antagonists. The author captures Jolyne's defiant, street-smart personality and Makima's manipulative nature effectively, staying true to their source material characterizations. The prose style is distinctive and evocative, with memorable phrases like "honey poured over gravel" and "shadows that look like collars." The imagery consistently reinforces the themes of control and imprisonment. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, particularly Jolyne's crude directness and Makima's deceptively pleasant manipulation. The story structure builds tension effectively through their verbal sparring, escalating to the psychological test in darkness before the final confrontation. The author shows strong understanding of both characters' powers and personalities, weaving Stone Free's string abilities naturally into the narrative. However, the piece suffers from some unclear moments, particularly the ending sequence where Jolyne "unstrings her own hand" - the mechanics and consequences of this action are confusing. Some metaphors become overwrought, and certain passages drift into purple prose territory. The pacing occasionally slows during Makima's philosophical questioning segments. The dialogue captures each character's voice well, though some of Makima's longer speeches feel slightly artificial. The emotional core remains strong throughout, with Jolyne's determination to resist control driving the narrative effectively. The piece avoids easy resolutions while maintaining narrative coherence. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Personal Statement: I did not believe in time until the first note appeared. It was a Tuesday. I had locked my desk drawer after leaving the containment floor. The drawer was standard issue, keyed to my badge, and I had the only key. When I returned the next morning, inside the drawer, on a single sheet of standard Foundation memo paper, was my own handwriting. NOTE 1: "Dr. Voss, Do not tell the ethics board. They will not help. The breach is not a failure of containment. It is a correction. You are the error. —Future Elara" I took the paper to Dr. Haddad, who measured ink bleed, paper stock, and pen pressure. The paper matched the batch in my locked cabinet. The handwriting matched mine within 94 percent confidence. The ink was dry. NOTE 2: "Stop checking the ink. Check the vents. SCP-████ has learned your sleep cycle. Do not open your mouth in the east corridor." Haddad laughed, then stopped. The east corridor had no ventilation anomalies. I checked. There was none. The Foundation formed a small review board. Dr. Lian asked whether the notes were a temporal anomaly. Dr. Orlov argued they were psychological manipulation by SCP-████, a memetic entity capable of inducing false confidence and self-recognition. Orlov said I should be monitored. I agreed, because I wanted to know which version of the truth was safer. They installed cameras in my quarters. They sealed my desk. They gave me a new memo pad and a locked box with two keys: one mine, one held by Site Security. Every night, I placed the box in the evidence locker. Every morning, I found a note inside, on standard Foundation memo paper, even though no one else had access to the paper. NOTE 3: "They are not trying to stop the breach. They are trying to make you the breach. Do not answer the phone after 0300. Do not read the name on the door. It is not your name." I did not read the name. I counted my steps to the door. I touched the plate. It said: Voss. I told Lian. She checked the plate. It said: Voss. Orlov checked. It said: Elara. The board considered three possibilities. First, a temporal anomaly: notes moving backward from a future where I survived the breach and tried to warn my past self. Second, a memetic attack by SCP-████, which had been observed to imitate trusted voices and create self-referential loops. Third, a psychological breakdown, induced by isolation and stress, producing confabulation. I was not comfortable with any of them. NOTE 4: "The third option is a lie. You are not breaking. You are being broken. The breach is already scheduled. Do not trust the timestamp. The note you are reading was written after the fire." There was no fire. But that night, I dreamed of smoke in the east corridor and a voice saying my name in my own voice. The next morning, the note was not in the box. It was on my pillow. The ink was warm. NOTE 5: "You are losing the thread. I am losing it faster. Do not go to the containment floor. Do not look at the monitor. The breach is not coming. It is being remembered into place. They have already opened the door. You are the one who opened it." Haddad ordered me to the containment floor. I went, because I was a researcher and because I needed to see what the notes meant. The containment cell for SCP-████ was sealed. The monitor showed a static field, then a face. It mouthed: Thank you. Lian said the notes were consistent with a closed timelike curve, but the contradictions made that unlikely. Orlov said the entity had been feeding me memories that were not mine, and the paper was a memetic anchor. Security found me unconscious in the east corridor. I checked the cameras. The footage showed me leaving my quarters. It also showed me staying in my quarters. Both timestamps were mine. NOTE 6: "Stop checking. The breach is not a door. It is a sentence. You are the sentence. Do not write your name. Do not sign the report. If you sign it, you become the note." I did not sign the report. I asked Lian to sign it. When I looked at the signature, it was mine. I began to doubt my own perception. I asked Haddad to test my memory. I failed. I could not remember my childhood surname. I could not remember why I had joined the Foundation. I remembered only the notes. NOTE 7: "You are almost here. I am almost you. The breach is a question the site keeps asking: who opened the door? The answer is the one who writes the report. Do not finish it. Do not let them finish it. The paper is not paper. The drawer is not locked. You are not safe." I locked the drawer. I locked the box. I locked my quarters. I sat in the dark and waited. The phone rang. I did not answer. At 0301, the note was in my hand. NOTE 8: "You answered. You always answer. The breach is not ahead of you. It is behind you. It is the report you are writing. It is the note you are holding. Do not be afraid. I am sorry. I am not sorry. The door is open. The door is you." I looked at the paper. It was standard Foundation memo paper. The box was locked. The key was in my pocket. I did not remember placing it there. I did not know if I had written it. I did not know if I would write it. I did not know if I was the researcher, the entity, or the future. The only thing I knew was that the note was real, because it was in my hand, and my hand was shaking, and the ink was dry. I began to write the report.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the Foundation universe and successfully creates an unsettling psychological horror narrative. The piece effectively employs the requested first-person perspective with interspersed notes, maintaining past tense throughout. The structure cleverly mirrors the protagonist's deteriorating mental state through increasingly fragmented and contradictory information. The writing excels in creating atmosphere and mounting dread. The progression from clinical Foundation documentation to existential horror is well-paced, with each note escalating the tension while introducing new layers of uncertainty. The author demonstrates strong command of the SCP format, incorporating believable Foundation procedures, personnel interactions, and containment protocols. The central conceit—notes from a future self warning of a breach—is executed with genuine creativity. The gradual revelation that the researcher may be both the source and target of the anomaly creates effective recursive horror. The contradictory information (door plates showing different names to different people, dual timestamps, conflicting camera footage) builds paranoia convincingly. Character actions remain believable throughout, with Dr. Voss responding rationally to increasingly irrational circumstances. The supporting characters (Haddad, Lian, Orlov) feel authentic to the Foundation setting. The voice remains consistent, maintaining clinical detachment even as reality fractures around the narrator. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overwrought territory, particularly in later notes where the language becomes somewhat purple ("The breach is a sentence. You are the sentence"). Some metaphysical concepts could be clearer—the exact nature of the temporal/memetic threat becomes muddied in the final act. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels slightly rushed given the careful buildup. The prose generally flows well, though some sentences feel artificially constructed for effect rather than natural expression. The imagery is vivid without being excessive, and the emotional complexity—doubt, fear, professional duty conflicting with self-preservation—rings true. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 78.0
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
SCP-7742 Object Class: Keter Special Containment Procedures: All confirmed SCP-7742 doors are to be walled in and monitored. No personnel are to open a door except approved expedition teams. Expedition teams are limited to six members and must carry two-way audio, motion sensors, and one (1) Foundation identification badge. If team members observe figures in white protective suits removing materials from the Archive, they are to retreat immediately and report the coordinates. Description: SCP-7742 designates a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide. As of ██/██/20██, 31 doors have been confirmed. Each door is 0.9 m wide by 2.1 m tall, constructed of brushed steel, and fitted with a single brass doorknob. All doors share identical scratches around the doorknob area: seven shallow parallel gouges, 3 cm apart, oriented at a 17-degree angle. The scratches show no tool marks, rust, or wear, and reappear on newly discovered doors within 48 hours of Foundation access. Opening any SCP-7742 door reveals a corridor leading to a vast archive extending beyond measurable space. The archive contains shelves, reading rooms, sealed vaults, and documents in at least 214 known scripts. Architectural surveys indicate internal volumes exceeding the exterior building by factors of 10^6. The environment remains at 18°C and 40% humidity. Documents within the archive reference a previous global civilization known as the "Covenant of Closed Rooms." This civilization appears to have been destroyed by a containment failure described as the "Unsealing." Several recovered documents use terminology closely matching Foundation procedures, but attribute them to an organization called the "Loom." The archive responds to Foundation personnel by altering documents. In three cases, files changed names to match staff present, while preserving old dates. Team members have reported the smell of wet paper and ozone, and a persistent impression that they are being read rather than observed. The doors do not age. Exploration Log 7742-1: Team 8921, led by Dr. Aris Vane, entered SCP-7742 through a door in an abandoned textile mill in ██████, Poland. 00:00: The team observed the door's identical scratches around the doorknob area. Dr. Vane recorded that the scratches "looked like someone had tried to open the door from the inside, but the marks are on the outside." The door opened without force. 00:14: The team entered a corridor lined with gray stone. The corridor ended in a vaulted reading hall. Shelves rose beyond visible height. No ceiling was found. A sign above the far entrance read: "THE LOOM, MEMORY WING." 00:32: Team member Dr. Lena Osei located a filing cabinet labeled "PERSONNEL, CURRENT CYCLE." She removed a personnel file bearing her name, photograph, and Foundation employee number. The document was dated 1642 and described her as "Archivist, Seventh Wing, appointed after the Unsealing." Dr. Osei reported no memory of prior service but stated her handwriting matched the signature line. 00:58: The team discovered a second cabinet containing personnel files for several current Foundation staff, including Dr. Vane and Site Director ██████. Each file contained the individual's current biometric data, but dates ranging from 1204 to 1901. One file listed Dr. Vane as "Senior Warden of the Loom, terminated for opening the Seventh Door." 01:20: Dr. Vane found a sealed ledger marked "O5 EYES ONLY." The ledger contained entries in modern English and Foundation shorthand. One entry read: "O5-4 entered without authorization. He asked for the name of the first O5. The archive gave no answer. He wept." Another entry, dated 1931, bore the signature of O5-9, then identified in recovered Foundation records as a child. A third entry, dated three days before the expedition, read: "O5-12 came alone. I do not know how she knew the door was here. She took a folder and did not look back." 01:47: The team observed three entities in white hazmat-style suits moving through a side aisle. The entities carried metal trays and removed documents from shelves. Their faces were obscured by reflective visors. They did not appear to notice the team until Dr. Osei stepped forward. The entities immediately dropped the trays and fled deeper into the archive, moving faster than humanly possible. Dr. Vane ordered retreat. 02:03: The team recovered one document from a fallen tray. The document was labeled "CONTAINMENT FAILURE 001: THE UNSEALING." It described a previous global civilization's attempt to contain a "door that remembers" and the resulting collapse of all governments, languages, and calendars. The document concluded: "The Loom survived only because it forgot itself." 02:11: The team returned through the corridor. Upon exiting, the door was sealed by an automatic steel plate. The identical scratches around the doorknob area had increased to nine. Recovered Document Excerpts: Document 7742-A: "Memorandum of the Loom, dated 1712" "To all Wardens: The Covenant is finished. The Unsealing has passed through every city. If the Loom endures, it must do so under another name, another flag, another century. Do not seek the Archive. The Archive is already seeking you." Document 7742-B: Personnel File of Dr. Lena Osei, dated 1642 "Role: Archivist. Cause of appointment: Voluntary memory surrender following the Unsealing. Note: Subject recognizes the door by the scratches. Do not allow Subject to count the scratches again." Document 7742-C: O5 Ledger Entry, undated "I entered without authorization. I wore no badge. I spoke no name. The shelves rearranged themselves around me, and I found a file with my own face on it. The date was before my mother was born. I am certain the Foundation is not the first to build this wall." Addendum 7742-1: Site Director ██████ has requested immediate review of O5-4, O5-9, and O5-12. O5-4 denied visiting SCP-7742. O5-9 could not be located for 72 hours. O5-12 submitted a resignation, then withdrew it. The resignation contained one sentence: "I took a folder. I am not returning it." Addendum 7742-2: As of ██/██/20██, the door in Poland has vanished. A new door appeared in the Foundation's own abandoned Sub-Site ██, with the identical scratches around the doorknob area. The Foundation has classified related audio as Level 4.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates strong adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while weaving together multiple narrative threads effectively. The author successfully captures the bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP entries, maintaining consistency throughout the technical descriptions, exploration logs, and recovered documents. The piece excels in world-building and conceptual creativity. The idea of a cyclical organization that forgets and reinvents itself across centuries is genuinely unsettling and original. The detail of identical scratches that increase in number, the entities in hazmat suits fleeing when observed, and the archive that "reads" its visitors rather than being read creates a compelling sense of cosmic horror. The exploration log format works well, providing natural pacing and building tension through timestamped discoveries. The revelation that current Foundation personnel have files dating back centuries, and that O5 Council members have been secretly visiting, creates effective paranoia about institutional memory and identity. However, the piece suffers from some structural issues. The transitions between different document types occasionally feel abrupt, and some revelations lack sufficient buildup. The characterization, while appropriate for the clinical SCP format, remains quite thin - team members function more as vessels for discovery than as individuals with distinct personalities. The prose is generally clean and purposeful, though it occasionally relies too heavily on mysterious implications rather than concrete details. Some elements, like the specific measurements and technical specifications, feel authentic to the SCP format but don't always serve the narrative tension. The ending maintains appropriate ambiguity while delivering a satisfying sense of escalation with the door appearing in the Foundation's own facility. The final addendum about classified audio provides an effective ominous note without overexplaining.
